utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We will restart. Counsel for the Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, might the witness Sead Ambeskovic be brought in, please? SEAD AMBESKOVIC, recalled

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambeskovic, please be seated. Can you hear the interpretation? Are you hearing everything clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Did you have a good night's sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much. I had a very good night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Ambeskovic, can you recall that back in September/October of last year that Miss Hollis and Mr. Paepen from the Prosecutor's office came to you and took from you a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of taking that statement did those two people from the office of the Prosecutor ask you to complete for them a sketch of the camp at Susica and, I think, also at Batkovic as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following my explanation and following my description of the map of Susica, I myself decided to make a sketch and then they said: "Well, go on and make a sketch so as to make it clearer what the layout was".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you look at the document that I now give to you? (Handed). Is that a photocopy of the plan that you yourself drew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the copy of what I drew myself, following the making of my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of Mr. Dixon, if it pleases your Honour, could you place that on the machine and I would like you to, going from the numbers that you have there, point to each number with your pen, and when you place your pen on the part of the plan where the number is, would you just explain to the Tribunal what each part represents? Could you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will show you. Let me see. Here this was the entrance, that is No. 8, and this is the camp itself. This was the electricity pole. This is where we were brought and beaten, tied to the poll and beaten. This building here was the, rather, this was something like a bunker and there was a machine gun, a heavy machine gun, pointed towards the door of the hangar, so this No. 7. Then this is the guard house, the guard house. This was Dragan Nikolic's office, one might say. This was the hangar in which we were placed and held. There were two doors, one door here. This was the entrance door and this door, the back door, was locked. This was the hangar, No. 4 now, this was the hangar next to it, some 10 to 15 metres away from the hangar in which the detainees were held. Under No. 5, No. 5 was, as I said yesterday, this was a shed, a utility shed, for unused or disused parts and material left by the territorial army. So there was some equipment there. No. 6 was the toilet, that was where we were taken and we were allowed to go out to the toilet. At the circles, little circles, are the guard posts or sentry posts. This is during our stay. That is where the sentries were placed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not clearly shown on that plan, but could you just indicate the direction of where the Susica River is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The river was down there, outside, outside the camp. It flows under the bridge and it goes this way, so this is the river. There was not enough paper when I was drawing this so I could not locate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. I have finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would like to draw your attention and the witness's attention to the fact -- do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Fine -- it is the first time that you mention the presence of the machine guns. I think that is a rather important element, and the witnesses could not have seen it before. So it is not in Rule 61 to carry out an investigation. I just want to point it out for your further investigation. I want to have the witness confirm the presence of point 2, item 2, on the map which seems to be the stationing point of the machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Perhaps the witness might be shown the plan again? I am not sure that No. 2 was the machine gun. I may have said that was the -- I think it is No. 7 but I will check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Sorry, that is right, but my question remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Let me repeat this. At No. 7, that was the placement for a heavy machine gun pointing towards the entrance door to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Any other machine guns in the sentry posts? Were there any other guns in those guard places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] No, this was the only machine gun, heavy machine gun, but of course the sentries in their sentry posts, they had their own weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The guards were armed at all times that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were armed all the time, all the time while they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This machine gun place, where the heavy machine gun was placed, was that there from your recollection the whole time that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was there all the time as long I was there. There was always one man manning -- one of the guards was manning the placement and the machine gun day and night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I am finished with that exhibit. Another thing about the statement that you gave, Mr. Ambeskovic, to the investigators from the office of the Prosecutor, I think in that statement you said that you were taken to the Susica camp on 13th June 1992, but I think yesterday in your evidence you said it was 11th June. Was 13th June the wrong date or was 11th June the wrong date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 13th June was wrong because I was making my statement in Tuzla, and when the statement was being read to me there was a mistake, an error was made in the writing, and I then corrected myself, and I think this was corrected eventually. The 11th June is correct the date, the 11th at 1830, eighteen hours and 30 minutes, 6.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the events that took place in the camp at Susica, Mr. Ambeskovic, I am wondering if you could recall an incident when you were taken out of the hangar with a man called Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that incident. This was in the morning hours, around 8 o'clock. Dragan Nikolic came in and also Majstorovic. They told us to get out, the two of us, myself and Osmanovic, and then they took us to that electricity pylon, the A pylon, the A electricity pole. They ordered us to kneel down and to put our hands behind our heads like this, so that is what they asked us to do, to kneel down and put our hands behind our heads. Then after that they said: "Where are your weapons? Who has weapons?" They asked us again to identify people who had weapons and they started beating us. They had rifles in their hands, also batons or truncheons. They started hitting us but I could not answer anything because I did not know anything about any weapons. I had no weapons myself so I just could not answer their question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did they beat you for at that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was about 30 minutes, if I can remember correctly, some 30 minutes, that the beating went on until we actually fainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they hit you, can you remember at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they hit us on the head, all over the body, the upper part of the body, kidneys, legs, and as we fell down they also continued kicking us with their shoes, trampling on the chest or hitting on the head, and I lost three teeth on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to losing three teeth, did you suffer any other injury at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had some injuries or wounds on the head. There were cuts on -- this was from the gun, the rifle hitting. Also I had -- I was full of bruises in the area of my kidneys and on the chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any broken bones at that stage as a result of that beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, three -- my three ribs were broken. That was later, the second time when we regained consciousness. When we regained consciousness they started hitting us again and then my three ribs broke in this part here. (Indicating) [Pointing to that part] Here. The three lower ribs. After that they started hitting us again, as I said, and we -- I fainted again. They brought water, they poured water over us and we came back, regained consciousness, and then they left towards Suad Mahmutovic, Nurija and Mirsad who were standing by the hangar facing in our direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do with those other people you have just mentioned, Suad Mahmutovic and Nurija, what happened to those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They started asking them again. I did not quite hear what they asked them. They again started beating them. That is what I could see. They started beating them, in the same way as I us with the rifles, with the rifle butts, with the batons and truncheons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that three men, was it, that were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was Suad, Mirsad and Nurija, three brothers, in fact. They actually were standing by the door of the hangar and they were leaning with their backs against the hangar wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another man there by the name of Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. He was also, he was standing next to us. This was again, this was by the door of the hangar in which we were kept. He was surrounded or he was in the company of two people who started beating him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was involved in the beating of the three brothers, Suad, Mirsad and Nurija Mahmutovic? Who was involved, who was doing those beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was there, then Goran, Goce, he was there. When there was Luka Majstorovic and Golijan, Nedeljko Golijan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was involved in beating the man Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were two people, as far as I could judge. They were from Sekovici. Those were the people I did not know. I only heard that they came from the village of Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see them beating the man Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that very well. When they left us they came to Nurija, Suad and that group, they were beating them and they were beating Zekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? What happened next after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they -- after four or five minutes, they took us back to the hangar, back to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to walk on your own or did you have to be assisted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we could not walk on our own. We needed assistance, so they invited -- they asked two people, of the inmates, from the hangar to take us into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were, we came to our positions, to our assigned places, not far from the door, some two to three metres from the door. We lay down on the concrete floor. I saw as we, as I was returning to my place, I saw a bus driving by full of people, and then another vehicle, another -- an excavator, a digging machine, that came after behind the bus and they went in the direction of Tisca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw this bus and the excavator on the road outside of the camp, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was outside of the camp because the road passes by the main gate. The gate was open and I could see the road, although I was inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please clarify what you mean by "what happened"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see or hear in relation to that bus as it drove past with the excavator? Did you just merely see it go past and that was the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after that I was in the hangar, not far from the door, about some 15 to 20 minutes later we heard bursts of fire not far from the hangar, some two to three kilometres away. That was the kind of distance which I judged because you could hear the shooting. And following the shooting, some 15 minutes later, the bus came back and the excavator came back following the bus and they returned along the same road on which they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that at the time immediately after you were taken in after this beating or was it at some other time that this happened, that you made this observation in the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was some, let us say, 20 minutes, 20, 25 minutes, following the beating and following our return to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The three men, the three brothers, Suad, Mirsad and Nurija Mahmutovic, did you see them come back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were returned into the hangar, let us say, an hour after us. So, Suad, all three of them, were brought back and Zekic, the fourth, was also brought?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they able to be walk in on their own account or were they carried in or how were they brought back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could not walk, they were very badly beaten. Three people left the hangar and they brought them in. They carried them in, first, Mirsad, then Zekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What condition were they in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were badly beaten, you could see that, and in this situation, I was not there, I was very close to them to see how badly beaten they were, whether they were unconscious, but I think they were conscious, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember two men at the camp, Dzevad Saric and Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember them. I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember anything happening to them at the time when you were in Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken out. One day Dragan Nikolic came, opened the door of the hangar, entered, called the names of Dzevad Saric and Smajlovic and asked them to come out. After that they were in front of the hangar and they -- the guards started beating them. We heard -- I was close to the door -- I heard their screaming and wailing, and some 30 minutes later these people were carried into the hangar because they could not walk on their own. They were carried by two people who were close to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall some time later, some three or four days later, the guards, Majstorovic and Dragan Bastah, coming to the hangar in order to take people out for work duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came in the morning, at about 10 o'clock in the morning. Dragan Bastah came and took out 10 men to take them to forced labour. Mirko Majstorovic was there. In his presence that happened. He chose 10 men and took them to a car. His car was parked on the road next to the bridge. It was a refrigerator truck. He put them in the refrigerator truck and drove them in the direction of Vlasenica. At about 6 o' clock in the evening he came back, brought them back, and I could see looking at these men, and one of them was next to me, they had been beaten at their work. They had been beaten as they were doing forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also remember when you were at Susica camp a man with the first name "Reuf"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember Reuf -- Reuf?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember Reuf. I know him very well. He worked with me in the same company. He was a car mechanic. I remember him quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall anything happening to him at the time you were in Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day he came -- Dragan Nikolic also came. They started to beat him inside and then he took him out. He swore at him. He cursed him, abusing him, his religion. He probably had something to ask him and he asked him about his brother. He took him out. I knew Reuf from before. He was a weak man. His arm had been broken prior to that and he had not quite recovered by that time. He was beaten outside the hangar about five or six metres from the door. We could see that. He kept beating him and asking him where his brother was. He did not know where his brother was. He could not answer that question. He kept saying: "I do not know where he is."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he kept beating him", who was beating him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic personally, himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this man Reuf when he came back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he could not walk on his own. The two men carried him in. He was beaten up. He was badly beaten. There was blood running out of his nose. His face was covered with bruises from the blows. He had also been kicked. He had difficulty breathing. It is only -- it was only three or four hours after that that he came round. He had fainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some days later, or some day later, were you again called out with Hajrudin Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. Osmanovic and myself were taken out. Hajrudin Osmanovic, his first name is Hajrudin. We were taken outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic came again. There was also Majstorovic there. They took us out just in front of the hangar. They again cursed at us: "Have you remembered where are your rifles?" they asked. "Who has weapons?" However, we could not answer that question because during the prior beatings we could not say anything because we did not know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how long after in terms of days or hours this beating took place from the beating where you had your ribs broken and your teeth knocked out, how long after was this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened two days after the first beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall there being two men in the camp by the name of Asim Zildzic and Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember these people quite well. I knew them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall a particular incident in relation to something that happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken out in the evening, I cannot quite remember the time because I did not have a watch on. They were taken out in the evening, Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic came accompanied by Majstorovic. They came in. They called Durmo Handzic's name and Asim Zildzic's name too. They took them out. As far as I could hear, it was just down the hill from the hangar because we could hear that. We could hear their screams and moans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained there for a long time. The beating went on for a long time. In my opinion, it lasted for about an hour or an hour and a half. After that people from the hangar, they called some people from the hangar to take them in. First, they brought Durmo and then they went back to fetch Asim. They put Asim right next to me, where I was. So one eye was sticking out, completely gouged out. His face could not be recognised from the beating. It was completely blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his eye was "gouged out" can you be a bit specific as to what happened to his eye and which eye it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the left eye. It had come out of the cavity. It was simply not there, not in its place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it still connected or was it gone altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was some tissue and it hung on this tissue just beneath the eye, the eye socket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few minutes after that, after they were taken in, he died. He died, and remained there until the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was beside you when he died, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he died in my arms. After that we just moved him about half a metre from there and we covered him. Then in the morning, as far as I can remember, about 4 a.m. they carried him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Durmo Handzic? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Durmo Handzic that night survived that night until the morning. Asim was carried out and buried. They called Hasim and his brother. They carried him and buried him. While Durmo remained there, his body remained there until about 9 o'clock, I cannot quite remember, 9.00 or 10.00. Majstorovic -- he asked Majstorovic to let him out, but he said that he could not do that without Dragan Nikolic's approval, and would not speak to him any more. Perhaps 20 minutes after that Dragan Nikolic came. Durmo asked him: "Please let me out so I can catch some fresh air". He told him: "You are going to die slowly, you will never go out", and kicked him in the chest and knocked Durmo over. Five or six minutes after that Durmo died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after Durmo died? What did they do with his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took out the bodies later, since they had closed the door immediately, there was the sound of a car approaching, and they also took him away to bury him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some days later do you recall Dzevad Saric and Nusret Zekic being taken out again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. That was during the night about 1.30 a.m.. Dragan Nikolic came in. Mirko Majstorovic was there too. They came in. They started shouting, cursing us, and asking: "Who tried to escape?" After that they had Dzevad Zaric stand up and Kolarevic and another man from Papraca whose name I do not remember. Also on the way out they picked up Zekic Nusret who was in the corner right next to the door. Perhaps five or six minutes after that we could hear the sound of a shot, of a gun shot, and there was another shot just down the hill from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning at about 5 o'clock we heard the sound of a car because nobody could sleep that night. I personally heard the sound of a car, of an engine. The car came right outside the hangar. The engine was turned off and maybe 15 minutes after that the car was started again and drove away. I know that they called out Hasim from the hangar -- Hasim Ferhatovic -- because his brother was outside so he was taken out too. Probably they took them to bury the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see those men again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. I never saw them again. Hasim told me that they had been killed since he was with me in the camp. In the morning when we got out to go to the toilet, next to the A tower I saw a big puddle of blood, and right underneath the hangar where we went by, as we were going to the toilet, I could see for myself and I was convinced that the men had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen whether or not that they had beaten the man Kolarevic before this day, Kolarevic before that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kolarevic -- I did not see Kolarevic being beaten and they had not taken him out prior to that time. He kept staying in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the man from Papraca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man who was not far away from me, they did not beat him either. I do not know if they had beaten him prior to that time. He was in a very bad condition. We were all dirty, of course. I do not know if he had been beaten before that time. I could not see him beaten during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a female being in the hangar called Saha Berbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Saha Berbic, yes, I do remember her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was she approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She could have been about 18, 19 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember something in relation to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Early evening, in one day in the early evening, Dragan Nikolic came himself, called Saha Berbic's name and she was there right next to the door. There were some other women with her there. She stood up thinking that he was going to ask her a question, but he told her to accompany him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did she do? What did she do when he said to accompany her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She tried to resist. She said she would not go; "Please", she said, "do not separate me from the other women". He came in, grabbed her by the arm and took her out. She resisted and also cried during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, about an hour after that, he brought her back to the hangar. Her hair was tussled and her clothes were torn. She was not far from me and the women asked her what had happened to her. She said that Dragan Nikolic had raped her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far were you from the women so that you could overhear this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, perhaps, a metre, one and a half metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from saying she was raped, did she say anything else had happened to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that she was taken out regularly every evening for two to three nights in succession, and after that she never returned to the hangar again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "she never returned to the hangar again", do you say you never saw her again or she just never came back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she was just not returned, and on one occasion when we were walking towards the toilet I saw her outside the guard house and she was washing the dishes. This was the last time I saw her, and never after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Nikolic's brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this moment, but I did know him. We were not very close but I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him at the camp site, at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a guard. He was a guard and I saw him at sentry post not far from the guard house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there from 11th June to the 3rd July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the circumstances of how it is that you came to leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One morning, it was on 3rd of July, we heard the door open around 7 o'clock in the morning. We heard the sounds of an engine, of a car engine, and outside the hangar we saw, near the bridge we saw a vehicle. Then Dragan Nikolic walked in, and Basic, I do not know his first name. They both walked in. They brought lists of people who were in the hangar, and they said: "You will be exchanged." And they started reading the names. They said: "As soon as your name is called you shall go out of the hangar". That was the order, so they started calling the names, and in front of the hangar there was a file of people, the file of soldiers in camouflage uniforms. They were lined from the hangar to the entrance into the bus. When my name was called I came out, and as I walked past the file of soldiers they started hitting me and they hit with the rifle butts, with truncheons and batons up to the point of entrance into the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Nikolic participate in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic had the lists of people in the hand, in his hands, and he was reading the names, so he was at the door, at the door just outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he did not participate in the beating as you went down through the cordon of men on either side towards the bus door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He was at the door and was busy reading the names, calling the names of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances -- where did you go then go? Where did the bus then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- the bus moved towards Vlasenica, and then we crossed the city and went towards Sekovici. The bus stopped at the bus station at one point and several more people who had been in the municipal prison were brought into the bus. This was Kemal Mutapcic and another man whose name I do not recall now. So they were brought into our bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus proceeded towards Sekovici and we had to be -- actually our hands were to be held behind our heads and our heads were to be down. We were not allowed to look out. As soon as we raised our heads we would be beaten immediately because there were six guards in the bus. They were sitting in the front of the bus and watching, and as soon as a head would emerge they would immediately start beating them. So they would beat us as soon as we raised our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from beating you, did they force you to do anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they forced us all the time to sing their Serbian nationalistic songs until we left the bus at Batkovic, so we were asked to sing all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you left the bus at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we stepped down, as we got off the bus, there were nets, iron nets, which prevented you from walking normally or from running, because again there was a lineup of soldiers from the door of the bus to the hangar, and again they were beating us as we were passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say nets, iron nets, can you just describe that a bit better so that we understand what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were reinforced concrete wires which were otherwise used for making reinforced concrete, and these were very thin -- very, very thick, rather, nets which would make it difficult for you to walk because your foot would get caught and you could fall, and as we fell we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The nets were on the ground and you had to walk over the top of them; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had to walk on them. They were rather flat on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that they were then people on either side of the nets who were beating you as you walked through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were lined up and from both sides, and they held batons and truncheons, various kinds of plastic pipes, also baseball bats, rifles. So these were the utensils with which they beat us as we walked past. Especially if you fell, when you fell then there was enough time for them to actually beat you so that you could not walk any further and people had to be carried, some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly outline the experience that you had for the time that you were in the camp at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can describe that briefly. As we entered into the hangar, since we were the second group to arrive, before us there was another group from Kalesije and from Papraca. So, as we entered we found our places in the hangar but all the time we were beaten until we came to our places. We were not allowed to move within the hangar. We were not allowed to move at all or to change the position, because in the middle of the hangar by the door there was a heavy machine gun which again was pointed at us in the hangar, so that we actually were not allowed to move, not allowed to make any movement whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten when you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, like everybody else, we would be taken out, and as soon as you were close to anybody who could beat you, they would beat you. For instance, when we -- each time that people came from Brcko, for instance, Zvornik, when these groups arrived, they were beaten and we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer an injury to your finger when you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was two days after my arrival. We were taken out to be interrogated, and the main person responsible for the camp was there. He -- and there was a pole outside the camp. We were taken to that pole and were interrogated. During the interrogation he actually cut my finger on my right hand. This was done with a knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you still have the scar from that injury today, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one can see it still. I do not know whether you can see it like this, but it is there. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Batkovic for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Batkovic until 20th, 21st July 1993, and also for a certain amount of time we went to work for -- to do forced labour at Lopare, Piper, Ugljevik, Stup.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] What was the type of forced work that you had to do? What sort of work did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was mostly heavy manual labour, cutting wood, felling trees, dragging lumber, timber, also weeding, weeding maize fields, agricultural work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have to do any work at any particular time when you were at Batkovic in relation to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they took us also to dig trenches, trenches for their army, and this was on the battle front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you would wish to mention now about the time that you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I could mention a few items, such as the first thing that happened when we arrived after the beating in the hangar, two people died actually as a result of that beating. They were the men that I used to know, and they died from this beating and were taken towards Bjelina in a car. This was Idriz Gopcic, and again I do not remember the second name. At the moment it escapes me. Then after that there were other people who were beaten on arrival, even when the International Red Cross arrived, and these were people hidden from the International Red Cross. Also, there were children and elderly people with us -- elderly people, I mean over 60 -- and when the Red Cross was due to arrive, they would be taken in a bus away from the camp until the representatives of the International Red Cross left and when they left the people were returned back to the hangar where they were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you, counsel for the Prosecutor. I look at my colleagues to see what questions they have. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. Mr. Ambeskovic, you told us 11 yesterday that after you were taken to the Susica camp where you were beaten, you were taken to the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. From the moment of entry into the camp area we were beaten. Then we were also taken to the office of Dragan Nikolic. This was the guard house and his office. After that -- there they asked our name, surname, year of birth, and they took us to the hangar where they also searched us. That is when they took all our belongings, money, and things like documents, valuables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your drawing, this hangar is pointed out as No. 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is No. 1, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that when you entered this hangar you saw children, women and elderly people there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They were very close to the entrance to the gate, to the door to the hangar. They were just by the door, and they remained in that place for the whole of the time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Close to the entrance door, because there are two doors here; one is the locked door, the other is the entrance door. They were close to the entrance door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can show you on this drawing. This was the entrance door and this door here in the back was locked, and locked with chains even, and you could not open that. But these women and elderly people were here, next to the door or entrance door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know the children. I did not know their names, not every child, but I knew the women who were there and again I did not know every woman, but I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am going to ask you about the women, but I would like to know the children, how old they were, little kids, young people, boys, girls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were about 10 or 11 years old, children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Boys, girls, only boys, only girls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were both boys and girls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they allowed to go out to the toilet or they could remain inside the hangar all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did let them out from time to time during the day, and go to the toilet and come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The women were the mothers of these kids?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they went out with their mothers or alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went out with their mothers. They allowed their mothers to accompany them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their mothers of these kids, did you know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not quite closely, but I did know them, almost all. There was a woman there too of about 90 years of age, very old lady, together with these other women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them, because you told us about a young woman that was raped, according to her testimony to you, by Nikolic, but what happened with the others? That case of rape was one case, or you knew about other cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not take out the other women. They were there too but he did not take them out. He came once and took her out, and the second time when he took her out she did not come back to the hangar and did not stay in the hangar after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if something happened to that old lady who was there in the hangar, something special?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic on a couple of occasions came and abused the old lady, told her that he would like to make love to her. Several times he came, cursed at her when she asked for water or something else. After I left I do not know what happened to that lady, after my departure from the Susica camp to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She remained there in Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she did. I do not know what happened to her later. Whether she was released, whether she ended up in free territory, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other women, did they also remain there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained there too, the women and the children. I do not know if they were transferred to the free territory, because only the men were transferred to the Batkovic camp, and the women remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the women, elderly people and children receive better food than you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they did not. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you, Mr. Ambeskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there somebody else responsible for the camp than Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Dragan Nikolic was there. He was in charge of the camp. He was the number one person in charge of the camp. He was connected with the people who were responsible to him. I cannot quite remember their names. I cannot remember the name. He was in charge of the camps and the military in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everybody was under his orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When there were these beatings you mentioned, was he present? You said he would be reading the lists sometimes of the people going out and they would receive beatings all the way. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from time to time. He read the lists of people who were in the hangar, and also when the when new groups were brought he would read the names to check if all the people were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these groups which came, what was the average age of most of them and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group of people came who said they had come from the central prison in Vlasenica. The average age was about between 28 years and 35.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned also there were children among them, were there many children and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, when the women from Vlasenica came there were a lot of women and children and, perhaps, one or two days after that they were transported in the direction of Kladanj, and I do not know what happened, but most of the women remained in the hangar where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While bringing these groups, was there any announcement of the things they committed, whether they thought it was certain acts or crimes, was there a specification of the acts they committed or were they just brought in for no reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not say anything about their acts. They just brought the people in -- the women and the children too. They brought them to the camp. After that they would take but the women and the children and the men stayed behind in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Ambeskovic, when you related the death of Asim Zildzic, you are the only one who mentioned this particular barbaric act of the eye that fell out of the socket. I suppose you were next to him when Asim came back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They brought him right next to me because on the way to his sleeping place was available, was free, he was practically right next to my feet. Then I approached him to see if he was still alive. At that moment I felt that he was still alive, maybe five or six minutes. I could see everything, everything that had happened to him, and five or six minutes after that he died.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. I look towards the counsel for the Prosecutor who is aware of this incident which is the first we hear of this nature. There are a lot of other witnesses and we will not hear all the witnesses. It is not right now my responsibility of saying what information you have received from the other witnesses. I would just like to draw attention to the fact that this incident of the eye out of its socket must be confirmed through other witnesses as well. That is the first comment I wish to make. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Excuse me, Mr. President, it is also the first time we heard about the rape, the other incident that we heard this morning for the first time, the rape of this young woman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. So these are points which must be confirmed, must be verified. I would like to draw your attention to it, unless you, counsel of the Prosecutor, would like to add some supplementary information right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends upon what witnesses see and observe; not all witnesses see the same things. I can only rely upon the evidence of the witnesses and what they tell us. There may be another witness that gives some evidence of the eye incident, but we are in the hands of the evidence of the witnesses. If one witness says he saw something and other witnesses did not see it, it may or not be that it happened; it could well be that the other witnesses did not see it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I understand and not everybody -- we are aware of what you are saying, but if I ask for this confirmation in addition to the information of my neighbour judge, when we heard of the death of these unfortunate detainees, the different testimonies are relatively similar of Asim who was going to die. They were all relatively close to him. It seems to me common sense dictates that if you have an eye that has dropped out of its socket, it is something you remember. I do not wish to further the investigation. It is merely a comment which the Tribunal, just like the one of the rape, wishes to make after hearing this testimony. I would like to ask Mr. Ambeskovic another question which is more general in nature. (To the witness): Firstly, do you have any other points you wish to raise or add to what you have said about the time when you were in the detention in the two camps lasting for about a year? Do you want to add something which you think is important to give us more information on the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes. I would mention again the Susica camp where we stayed from the 11th June to 3rd of July. The conditions were horrible; you could hardly call them conditions. For instance, in 15 minutes 700 people had to go out to the toilet and come back; and the maltreatment, the shooting in the hangar itself; the closing of the windows that could have been used for ventilation, practically it was strangulation and suffocation because there was not enough air for the 700 people in the hangar; the food we did not get, we received very, very small quantities of food, it was bad most of the time; the conditions, the lack of cleanliness, the dirt; we had gotten lice, all of us, at one point in time because we had nowhere to wash, to change our clothes, and it went on the whole time while we were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Before completing your testimony, the Tribunal would like to know what feelings you have now more than two years after the event, what do you feel now? What are your strongest feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel like all my other men who were with me. I came to testify so that this injustice to the people that was committed to be punished in some way or other. It was only after that that I will be satisfied and I will feel better.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Ambeskovic, we thank you very much. We are very grateful that you have come. We are fully aware of the difficult conditions, psychological difficulties above all, making you come here to give your testimony. I hope that when you go back you will find some inner peace and serenity. I think our investigation of this witness has now completed and I think he can now leave the room and go to the room specially reserved for him. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I suggest to all of you that we will adjourn right now and start again at 11.45. We stand adjourned. (Short Adjournment) (11.45 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We can resume the hearing, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, just before we call the next witness whom will be taken by my colleague Miss McHenry, there are two matters I would like to raise, if I may. Firstly, your Honours, I noticed when I came to court this morning that there was a photographer in the court who was taking what appeared to be close up photographs of the witnesses. Your Honours, this is perhaps an oversight on my part, but in so far as any -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. I saw that as well. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in so far as the non-disclosure order may not apply to someone taking photographs like that, I would ask it be extended to that because I do not think it is appropriate that witnesses should be photographed at such close range by people over whom we have no control. I realise that these witnesses are being videoed, but we have full control of that. I would ask that the order for non-disclosure be extended in all cases in respect of all witnesses so as to exclude photographers taking photographs in the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We have been discussing very, very briefly this particular point and I would like to now tell you what we both think about this point. This is a public hearing. We have stated that clearly. We were very concerned with the important question regarding the conditions in which the testimonies of the witnesses would take place. All the witnesses agreed and said that they would like to make public statements, public testimonies, and this is the reason why all the pictures from this hearing are made available from our cameras distributed throughout any TV network wherever in the world. Based on that particular consideration, we do have to recognise that the question of witnesses' protection as they wish it is not, in fact, assured as such, since the pictures from the video screen can themselves be photographed by photographers. So, the first conclusion that the Tribunal draws here is that it is not more dangerous for the witnesses when they are figured on TV screens throughout the world on the basis of the pictures made available from us. Let me correct you here, counsel for the Prosecution, on the question that we control the pictures in the Tribunal; we do not because they are made fully available to any TV station which is interested in them. This is fully available knowledge To the witnesses because they have all wished so far to appear unconcealed. So, that is the first point. It is not normal to prohibit access of photographers to the Tribunal. However, we are sensitive and we are aware of the importance of the points you have made regarding the presence of photographers. This can be a point of disturbance. These photographs are taken behind the back of the witnesses. This is a public hearing. It is accessible to the whole of the media in as far as any witness may not have objected to that point, and we think, the Trial Chamber, the Tribunal, is of the opinion that it is better, therefore, to prohibit the access of photographers during the testimony of the witnesses, however, remaining valid all the provisions that have been made public prior to the hearing. Subject to the control of the Registrar, the photographers may take photos at the beginning of the hearing. Is that correct Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Good. So in that case if the photographers wish to take pictures either of the public gallery or within the public gallery, they have to do that at the beginning of the hearing and then the hearing starts. So let me summarise the position as it is now. From the point at which a witness has accepted, and we are very aware of the importance of this question, on a case by case basis to appear unconcealed, then prohibiting photographers would be an illusion because in any case these pictures are made available throughout the world and without control of the Tribunal -- I would like to repeat that point -- without control, so video screens can be photographed. However, I think that the presence of photographers during the hearing can disturb the witness. The witness himself has made a great effort in accepting to be photographed by the cameras of the Tribunal. In that case, I think the conclusion would be that it would be better to prohibit photographs being taken during the testimony, during the hearing. That is difficult. It is a psychological problem. It is not very good and it is very unpleasant for the witness to have the feeling that they are being photographed from behind their back. So I would like to ask the Registrar to get in touch with security services to ensure that throughout the whole of the testimony of any witness there are no photographs taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please your Honour. Your Honours, you also raised another matter with the respect to the evidence of the last witness which I would like to touch upon, if I may? That deals specifically with the two issues raised about the evidence concerning the eye socket and the eye being out of the socket and the evidence pertaining to the young lady who was taken out by Nikolic. If your Honours please, in our submission, I was reluctant to go into too much detail in the presence of the witness in response to your Honour's questions for fear that the witness may feel that we in some way or other doubted his testimony on both those issues. But, if I may, I would like to say that, in our submission, this evidence does not require corroboration on our submission for the purposes of either proof beyond reasonable or, indeed, and less so for this hearing, either of those issues do not go directly to proof of the charge. They are mere evidence surrounding the circumstances. In relation to that, may I say that the conditions under which these unfortunate witnesses found themselves were such that their recollection of events would vary among them and themselves would probably from time to time have faded or changed or may have been affected by what they saw. It is, indeed, a well recognised fact that a group of people looking at an incident can see a whole range of things happening. It does not in any way, in my submission, affect the credibility of what they say; it merely means that some people see some things that other people do not see. Indeed, when that is overlaid by terror, by a feeling of imminent death, by a feeling that if one raises one's head to look at what happens that could bring upon them consequences of the most horrible kind, then it is perfectly understandable, in our submission, that some witnesses would see some things which other witnesses would not see. Finally, in my submission, it is regrettable that this issue arose in the presence of the witness because, indeed, there are three other witnesses who speak of the incident with relation to the eye socket. It would be regrettable if the witness felt that somehow or other just because he came first in time and ahead of these other three witnesses that somehow or other what he said was not regarded as truthful. Indeed, a similar situation may well apply with respect to Nikolic taking the lady out, because this witness gave evidence of his proximity to the people, to the women, and his ability to hear the conversation. It is perfectly conceivable that he is the only witness that heard this conversation. Indeed, if he is the only witness that heard the conversation, there is no requirement of corroboration and, in my submission, there is no reason, having regard to the circumstances, that that evidence should in any way be doubted. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, that possibility of asking questions must be limited, do I deduce it from your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all, your Honour. I am merely responding to what your Honour raised with respect to that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. I would like to point out that the Tribunal, according to our rules of procedure, wants to ask all the questions which we think are necessary so that we can fully evaluate the fact. If I and Madam, the judge, would like to ask that question, it is because we felt that it was relevant. Of course, I understand your concern, you say we still have three witnesses, and the witnesses might deduce or, rather, find out what is going on after that testimony, but counsel for the Prosecutors, the witnesses all know each other, they live together, they are neighbours. So, I am sure for a long time they have talked at length of what they are going to say to the court. However, I do feel in order to fully understand the facts, it is important that the Tribunal can ask questions of such a significant nature, because this could lead to other questions which might, indeed, help you, counsel for the Defence. Perhaps the next time you might ask questions asking for further specification relating to the hangar. I am sure not everyone is seeing the same things. What you see is very personal and we are well aware of that. We looked at two points which we felt were particularly relevant in a place or in a space which is so restricted, where terror rained, events like rape or an eye out of its socket are incidents that will not remain unobserved. That is why we felt it was necessary to ask for further clarifications. If the next witnesses change their statements, the Tribunal cannot help it, but I do feel for good proceedings we could help the Prosecutor, because there are many other witnesses for everyone who listens to us today, we only are listening to 13 witnesses but there are many, many other witnesses, and I think it is normal that we must point it out to the bureau for the Prosecutor that some points need more information, because you could draw conclusions from that for further questions in this Tribunal and, perhaps, during other hearings. Thank you. Perhaps we can call upon the next witness whenever you think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the next witness, he does not wish to have any additional protection measures other than his address. Therefore, as with the other witnesses, I would ask that the protective order be lifted with respect to the Prosecution's next witness. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: [Original in French] I ask the Registrar to take note of this request from the bureau of the Prosecutor. The answer of the Tribunal, which is the same which we have had for the other witnesses, save the address and the photographs during the hearing of the witness. So as from now I would like to say which is the next witness that will be in the court?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Elvir Pasic. ELVIR PASIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, first of all, have you got the right language? Yes. Is it OK? Can you hear me clearly? Mr. Elvir Pasic, do you hear me? Please stand and read the oath which has been submitted to in your mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. You can sit down, Mr. Pasic. Before starting your testimony to the Prosecutor which has called you to come to give your evidence, the Tribunal would like to thank you. We are fully aware of the difficult conditions you had to face, a long travel and the psychological impact which meant you had to relive the memories of things, perhaps, you wish to forget. So thank you very much. Furthermore, we would like to tell you that you can give your evidence knowing that you are protected by the international court. At any moment during your testimony if you face any difficulties whatsoever, please inform us and we will try to do our utmost for you. Madam Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (To the witness): Sir, would you please tell the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Elvir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 28 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war where was your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to live at Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Rogatica an Opstina bordering the Opstina of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you live in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived at Rogatica for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period beginning around 1992, do you know approximately how large the population of Rogatica was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rogatica as a municipality or Opstina had some 26,000 inhabitants or citizens. The town itself had a population of about 8,000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that within the Opstina of Rogatica there was also a town called Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The Opstina of Rogatica includes also various villages surrounding the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate percentages of Muslim persons versus Serb persons versus Croat persons versus others within Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The percentages were roughly 70 per cent were Muslims, some 30 per cent were Serbs and others, other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war what was your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately before, on the eve of the war, I was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period did you have any connection with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to work as a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court how often you worked as a reserve police officer and whether there came a time when your police work increased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period just before the war I used to work every day as the same as a regular police. I used to work for eight hours every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that time where you worked every day, how often did you work as a reserve police officer, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time following my army service, I was invited to military drilling or training once a year as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you started work working full time as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in early September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you started work full time, did you ask to start work full time or were you called upon to do that? Can you explain how that works?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me. They asked me to do that, to work full time for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a reserve policeman, I was under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and somebody from higher up asked that all reserve policemen should work full time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period when you first started working full time as a police officer, were there both Muslim police officers and Serb police officers working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when that changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later that changed altogether. The reserve policemen and even active policemen of the Serbian nationality refused to work with us, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what happened after they refused to work with the Muslim police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They refused to work with us in the same building. They refused to do the same kind of work and duties that we had, and soon after that they actually established their own police station which they called the police station of the Republic of Srpske, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then were there two Police Forces working within Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, yes, there were two Police Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how the two Police Forces worked separately, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the police stations, the Muslim station, was reporting to the Secretariat for the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we tried to do all our normal tasks that we would be doing under normal conditions in normal times. The second police station was the police station of the Republic of Srpske which controlled parts of the town by force. They decided that these were the parts of the town, the districts in the town, to be controlled by them, and it was very complicated to work under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the complications and tensions result in your making any decisions about future police work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two Police Forces could not remain; something had to be done to change this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue working for the Police Force after the separation happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that division of the two Police Forces, I continued to work for two to three days and then I stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do once you stopped working full time as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I starting working as a waiter again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when it was that you stopped acting as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was towards the end of March or beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting in the early spring of 1992, did you observe either during your police work or outside of your police work any activity involving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions I saw columns of army vehicles passing through the town, and then stopping and billeting not far from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about the areas where they would stop and billet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be stopping mostly in areas where the population was predominantly Serb. So they would spend sometime there, two to three hours, and then they would leave again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time where you saw some evidence of arms being transferred or being moved? Weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not present at any point where there would be some kind of transfer of arms, but whenever the trucks, army trucks, spent sometime in Serbian villages, when they left one could hear heavy shooting which meant that some weapons had remained in the villages. That was our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an incident while you were still working as a police officer where at a checkpoint you stopped a vehicle not from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one incident of this kind. I stopped a vehicle that had Macedonian licence plates, which was very surprising and unusual to see such cars with such licence plates in our town. When I stopped that vehicle the vehicle had five passengers; all five of them I knew personally. They were the residents of my town. Four of them were dressed in camouflage military uniforms and they had military regulation weapons, automatic submachine guns. The driver was the only one who was in civilian clothes. My first task as a reserve policeman was to ask for their documents, for the car driver's licence and the registration licence. The driver did not have the driver's licence, had no other documents -- no documents about the vehicle to prove the ownership of the vehicle. I asked him to get off -- to get out of the vehicle. I asked him where he was going. He said he was going to Borika. Borika is a village not far from Rogatica, mainly inhabited by the Serb population. I asked him to open the luggage compartment of the car, and when he did I saw a certain quantity, a larger quantity, of weapons and ammunition for which he had no papers or documents, which means that he was not allowed to drive such weapons on public roads. At that moment one of the uniformed passengers from the car also stepped out of the car, and I thought since he was armed that he would oppose me or that he would do something to me, and I was somewhat worried about my personal security. I told him to go back into the car. Then I released the driver as well and they drove off towards Borika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more specifically if you remember anything about the quantity or the kind of weapons that were in the trunk of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The quantity of weapons was roughly some 50 automatic submachine guns for infantry fighting; some two to three crates of ammunition for these submachine guns; there were also a few anti-tank grenades and a crate of hand grenades. All the weapons were new and, actually, this was the kind of weapons that I used in the Yugoslav National Army, JNA, at the time when I was doing my military service, so I concluded that this was the JNA weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened in Rogatica in late May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late May 1992, Rogatica came under fire, under shelling by Serbs from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the shelling lasted continuously for two to three days. Most of the population in the town was Muslim at that time, and they were trying to hide. They were in the centre of the City with more solidly built buildings so that they could find shelter from those -- from the shelling. Soon after that, electricity was interrupted, the electricity supply was interrupted. There was no telephone and no water supply. Then seven days later, five to seven days later, the so-called Serbian forces of Republic of Srpske, these were mainly people from Rogatica, Serb nationals of Rogatica, they came into the town asking the Muslim population to surrender to them, to become loyal to their government, until they, what they said, would clear the town from the so-called green beret and Muslim extremists, but there were no Muslim extremists in the town anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Serb military forces came into the town of Rogatica, did you see anything about any equipment they were using or operating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all were very well armed and well equipped with various kinds of weaponry, and this was the kind of weaponry that the JNA had used. They came with a transporter, with a personnel, armed personnel carrier, and the vehicle had the insignia of the JNA, and this was the olive green, drab olive green colour. They all had the uniforms which were practically identical with the uniforms of JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after there was this call to surrender and pledge loyalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
