utterances.text: The local population did not trust them because even before the call was made, while the electricity supply was still there, we were actually able to see on television what had happened in Zvornik, Bijeljina, Foca and other Muslim places, what happened to the Muslim population which had responded to the invitation of the Serbian authorities in those locations. So, and we saw that very -- so that very few people responded, some two to three families responded, usually of mixed marriages or those that had some Serbian member in the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the other people or families do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were all very excited and did not know quite what to do. For the most part, they were prepared to run away, to flee if an attack came, because we expected an attack, and some people barricaded themselves in their cellars thinking that, perhaps, the Serbs will not be able to destroy their houses or their cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any organised armed resistance during this period or any other period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Muslim side, there was no organised formation or armed formation that would, that could offer resistance to the possible aggressor, that is, the Serbs. At that time the town had some 50 to 70 men of Muslim nationality, who were armed with personal weapons, side weapons, maybe rifles which they used for hunting or for sport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those 50 to 70 men try to launch any sort of attack against the occupying forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not try to do anything at all, no attack. Their only objective was to stand in front of buildings where the Muslim population was heavily concentrated, and they said that if at one point the Serbian forces should try to attack or assault the building, that they would then try to defend the people who were in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So after that the shelling of Rogatica continued. Larger and larger grenades fell and much of the city was destroyed or damaged. Seven -- after seven days I was captured. I was captured by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the circumstances surrounding your capture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when I was captured I was in the cellar of my house in the building where I lived. The town had been heavily shelled, and at one point I noticed somebody, I heard steps, I heard somebody walking round the building. I was quite sure that there could not be any Muslim units and through the little window of the cellar I saw a Serbian soldier. Then they came into the cellar. There was some 50 Muslims in that cellar and they started shouting at us, shooting, and told us to get out of the building. As soon as we came out of the building, everything was clear. We were fully under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened after you were brought out of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came out of the building all women and children, some 25 of them, were put aside on one side and men, some 20 to 25, had to lie on the ground, lie on their stomachs and chests, put their hands behind their heads, and the soldiers who captured us started hitting us with whatever they could, kicking us, hitting us with rifle butts, with fists. They asked about our weapons which we did not have. Since I was in -- I was a part of a reserve Police Force and people who captured me knew me, they asked me to hand in my weapons, but I had given my weapons to the police when I have left the police. One of them wanted to cut my throat and then I said: "Well, I only have one, my personal pistol and I will give it to you", I told him. I went into my apartment accompanied by a soldier. I gave him my pistol and when I came back the children and the women were no longer there in front of the building, only my mother, my grandmother and my aunts were waiting for me while all the men were still lying on the ground with their hands tied behind their backs. Then I was the only man, the only man, perhaps because I handed in my weapon, they allowed me to go with the other women, with my mother, grandmother and aunt to go to the secondary school where all the women had been placed who were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed at the school 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you free to leave this school or were you being kept there forcibly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody could leave the school because that was very well secured by guards. The only thing we could do was go to the toilet and the central hall in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of administering that school and keeping you and the other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the men who guarded the school, I knew them personally because I had seen them in the town previously, and the man in charge of the school was Vlado Markovic who used to be an active policeman before the war in the police station in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his function was at this time in addition to being in charge of the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was captured a group of soldiers who had come to take me, they were under his command. That is what I knew at the time, but I now know that he was commander in chief of the entire unit that had been prepared and armed especially for cleansing the town of Muslim -- of the Muslim population which meant either deport or kill the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that this was part of a special unit and, if you know, do you know what this unit was called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit had no special label, name, but I do know it was a special unit because I had contact with people from that unit after I had left to the farm where I spent 20 days, and they told me that they were not under control of any big institution, but that Vlado was the chief and he was the one who decided what they should do. Their only task was to work around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how it was that after 20 days you left the school and were brought to the farmhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 10 days in the school the man in charge, self-appointed man in charge, of the Serbian forces, Rajko Kusic, in Rogatica came accompanied by his bodyguards and said that all of us Muslims who had been captured in the school must go to a territory where we had family, and this was the territory under the control of the Muslim forces, in fact, of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people had relatives, others did not. A list was to be made where each person would go, the name of the relatives, place, the address and the telephone number. The organisation was not so good, so the list was never drawn up. So next time they came, they just forced us to -- on to lorries and buses and drove us out of the town telling us that we were going to the free territory, that is, territory controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you brought to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as we were leaving the town all the vehicles were stopped and the soldiers in our escort made it clear to us that all the men over 18 years of age and under 60 years had to leave the vehicles. Unless they did it on their own, they would be killed, they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got off the lorries. There were 28 men, we were 28 in the convoy. The convoy continued on its way. I did not know at the time where they were heading, and we were held on the farm at the exit of the town. The main reason was to take care of our documents so we could go to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the reason or is that what they told you the reason was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what they told us. Of course, there was no reason to keep us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back for a minute. You just indicated that -- excuse my pronunciation -- Rajko Kusic, I believe you said, was in charge of the Serbs in the town after the attack and takeover; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had he played any role in the incident you described with the car full of weapons that you stopped at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His role was to come out of the car, without my approval, having weapons in his hands, that means my life was at risk, and all he said was: "What is this young man bothering us with?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the farmhouse that you were taken to after you left the school, how long did you stay at the farmhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the farmhouse 18 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many other, if any, detainees were kept at this farmhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to us, 28 of us, that stayed at the farm, there was a special room where there were three or four inmates, I am not quite sure. We did not have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the detainees, was the farmhouse used for any purpose other than keeping you and the other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the farm was used to accommodate a special unit that was tasked to do work around the town. One room was for sleeping and rest of those soldiers; another one was like an office where they planned their activities, and there was another room where they kept their weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened such that you left the farmhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day without any previous announcement they came with one lorry, brought a family, they came in a bus, brought a family in that bus, and told us to get on to the bus, so we could go to the free territory to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the men in the bus knew the road that we were following quite well. He claimed there was no way that we could reach the free territory going along that road. I could not believe him personally, because I was convinced that we were headed towards the free territory. However, he was right. We came to Vlasenica. Outside the police station we waited for two hours in Vlasenica for a decision to be made what to do with us. After that we headed towards Kladanj. It was already getting dark. Twelve kilometres from Vlasenica at the cross roads going to Sekovici and Kladanj, and the name popular name of that cross roads is Tisica, we were stopped by Serbs, Chetniks, whom I did not know. They got on the bus and wanted simply to kill us all off without any argument, without talking to us. After about an hour of waiting an argument between the Serbs stopped us and those who escorted us, it was decided that we should go back to the Susica camp in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the soldiers who were escorting you, in other words were they from the farmhouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were the same soldiers who had captured me personally, and who watched us in the school, who watched us at the farm. They escorted us along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back actually because I forgot to ask you before. When you were at the farm and you said it was used for these special forces, did you learn anything about exactly what these special forces would do or how frequently this special unit, how frequently they would leave to perform their work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I knew most of them or most of the men in the special unit, I had the opportunity as their captive to speak to them in a more relaxed environment. They went roughly every day or every other day to work. When they came back they were happy and they were telling stories how they had cleansed certain parts of the town of Muslims, how they had killed this and that individual in that street, how they set fire to a house, a house of one person or another, and similar activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people who were part of the special unit do you know what they had done before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had different occupations. Some of them were farmers, others were activity policemen, some were workers, factory workers, or shop assistants. It was a mix of different occupations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how were they dressed? Did they dress in civilian clothes or in some sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms, military uniforms, with a lot of pockets and space for different kinds of weapons and other equipment that they needed in their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me bring you to where you were, which was you said you were being brought to the Susica camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me first what happened when you were brought to Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way out of the bus which took us to the camp we were searched thoroughly, and everything that remotely resembled a weapon and anything that could help us to escape or some such activity was seized, and all the valuables were seized from us too; money, rings, watches or any similar objects and articles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you to ask were the valuables were taken. Were they ever returned to the people from whom they were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on, please, with what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we were taken into the actual camp, into the camp itself. The special unit from Rogatica had come that had brought us and we were handed over to the personnel that was in charge of the camp. They put us in a line, in a column in the camp. We were 29 men and two women. We had to stand there for about half an hour. There were in the camp about 200, maybe more than 200, previously captured women and men, many more women than men. After that a man came with two persons in his company. He looked like he commanded greater authority than the other two because he was in the middle, he was surrounded by them. He took a list of our names and said that we should find a place for ourselves and then he left. An hour after that, about an hour after that he came back to the room. He shouted really very loudly and had a knife in his hand and asked everybody whose knife it was. Of course nobody answered because the knife did not belong to any of those present, any of the inmates present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the person who was yelling and appeared to be in charge, did he at any point identify himself in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a little later he did identify himself. When he started hitting whatever he had in his hands, mostly it was the rifle butt, he kicked, he hit with his hands, he punched people and also using the blunt side of the knife he said he was, his name was Dragan and he was going to cut our throats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that he said this while he was beating. Can you describe how the beating was conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came up to me, asked my name and then when I told him what my name was he started using very ugly words about my nation, and hit me first with a slap, slapped me on the face, then he punched me, then he kicked me into my genitals, in my genitals. I was about to fall. One of the men in his company hit him in the chest with the rifle butt, and as I was bending he kicked me several times in the head. I fell down and he went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- were you able to see whether or not any of the other detainees were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us, the 28 men who came that night, were beaten up very, very badly. Others he did not hit at the time but he did beat them later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, I would like to ask the witness what exactly was Dragan Nikolic saying to you, what sort of insults? Did he, for example, defame or blaspheme against your religion? Can you tell us more precisely what exactly Dragan Nikolic said in terms of his insults?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said like this: "I fuck your mother", Balija is a derogative term, "You Muslims never existed, you never existed or will never exist. I will eradicate you, I will cut your throats, I will butcher you all" and similar abusive language.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you go on? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were beaten up he went out, the man who had introduced himself as Dragan and his two companions. In about an hour he came back again. He did not address us, but he walked up to the women who were captured, who were in the camp, mostly women between 25 and 30 years of age. He took out three of them outside. Of course they did not dare resist. He laughed and kept saying: "Don't worry you will have a good time with me." Those women came back maybe in about two, two and a half hours. They looked miserable, traumatized, depressive. They kept weeping. They did not dare tell anyone what had happened. It was clear to me that they had been sexually assaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that Dragan returned with his two companions and he entered the camp, and simply called two names which I do not remember at this moment; these were the names of inmates who had been there before we came. There were two young men, maybe my age. They looked very innocent. And he said that they had used to attack him before the war started, that he had some accounts to settle with them from before the war, such as: "You did not pay for my drinks in the cafe, you did not get up for me to sit down on the bus", or whatever. Then he came to them and then he beat them for a long time, a long time, and I could not watch -- believe me, I could not keep my eyes open. They remained on the floor, but I did not even dare to ask whether they were still alive or not. I do not know whether they were alive at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that he left and there was a lull, dawn was approaching, and I was simply waiting for the Rogatica special police, so because they promised they would come and get us in the morning and take us somewhere else. But before the special unit from Rogatica came, Dragan entered the room about 9 o'clock in the morning and, pointing his finger at 15 men who had been in the camp before we arrived, and he told them to go out and do work. They will be sent out to work. They put them on a small van and the van drove away. The women started weeping and sobbing as they left because they felt that the men would never come back. An hour after that, the special Rogatica police unit came who wanted to take us and to transport us and again Dragan was there. He was the one who read our names. That was the list that was prepared the night before. Each one of us had to go past him, say "Yes, that is my name", and at that moment he would either spit into our faces or would hit us with a fist, slap us in the face or do something like that, and said: "You can go now". So we sat in that car and when we were on the bus the bus proceeded on its way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the other detainees who had been there ever tell you anything about the knife that Dragan had come in with and accused someone in your group of having?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was so tense when he left the room after he had come with that knife and said somebody wanted to kill him with the knife and so on, we were all so frightened. But there were people who were brave enough to tell us: "Do not worry about this knife. This knife he has, he had already used 10 times always showing the same knife, Dragan showing the same knife, and always having the same story, 'This is the knife with which somebody wanted to kill me', so this was just a pretext for him to come to be able to beat us".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel when you were leaving Susica when you got on the lorry to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although I did not know where the bus was taking us, I was happy to have left and be -- and that I was no longer in the hands of the man called Dragan. That was the only feeling I had at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, in fact, were you brought when you left Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we boarded the bus, the Rogatica special unit soldiers told us that we would be exchanged. But on the way we were held at Sekovici for three to four hours. We were held up by the Serbian army control in Sekovici, the Sekovici region. So we waited for a long time and then it was decided that somebody from the Sekovici unit, together with the Rogatica soldiers, should accompany somewhere, but nobody told us where. In fact, we ended up in the Batkovic camp near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One year and five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that you were at Susica July 15th, and then from July 16th for the next period of time you were at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I arrived in the Batkovic camp on 16th July in the afternoon, around 5 o'clock p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe generally whether or not you witnessed any mistreatment while you were at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe generally the kinds of mistreatment that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I saw mass beatings by the Serbian soldiers who would be taking one, two to three people, detainees, and that they would take them out not far from the camp, and they would, some 10 people would be beating one person who was in no position to defend himself. Some of them died during the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who died as a result of beatings at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man from Bijeljina who was kept in the camp, everybody called him "Professor". I do not know his name, first or last name, but he died some eight hours after having been beaten. Two men, two elderly men, from Rogatica, from my native town, also died two days after having been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform any work while you were at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to do a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what kinds of work you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, instance of forced labour was collecting wood for the elite units in Bijeljina. We had to go to a town called Lopare, and we were accommodated in the local school, and every day we were taken to cut, to fell trees, to cut wood and so on. So we would work in the forest all morning, all day, rather, from 7.00 in the morning until 5.00 in the evening as long as daylight was there. Then we were taken back to the school and the following day the same procedure. Also, I was sent to the front lines to dig trenches for Serb soldiers, and I spent three months there. Otherwise, we were also asked to do some heavy work in the fields, in factories, where we were loading flour, sugar and similar things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the International Red Cross ever visit any of the places where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Red Cross came to the Batkovic camp in late August or early September. That was the first visit -- in 1992, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did anything happen prior to the Red Cross's visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the camp had a number of women over the age of 60 and under the age of 18, these people were always taken away just before the arrival of the Red Cross representatives. There were two buses and these people were taken away in these buses, together with them some 10 to 15 people who had been beaten more than others were also taken away, because they still had bruises, they had cuts, well, you could see the effects of beating, so they were taken with elderly and the young so, and to be returned after the departure of the Red Cross representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The elderly and young, were they men, women or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st June 1993. Sorry, the 21st July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release did you receive any medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after leaving the camp I spent five and a half to six months in the hospital, for the pulmonary diseases hospital, in Zagreb, Croatia. I had tuberculosis of the lungs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first realise you were sick; was it after you were released or while you were still being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt pain for the first time, the pain in my chest, in the beginning of January 1993. I was still in the camp at that time. I did not know it was tuberculosis but I had pain in the chest, and the pain was getting worse from day-to-day. Later I was told this was TBC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you told that you had tuberculosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to Zagreb two days after the release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were still being detained and you were feeling ill, did you attempt to seek medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when I could hardly move the pain was so severe, I did ask for medical help. The medical help consisted in me seeing a doctor in the army barracks of Bijeljina. There was a doctor there. I came to that doctor. He did not allow me to come closer to him than three metres. He asked me why I was reported and sent to him. I said: "I feel pain in my chest, in lungs". He gave me an injection and said that I should be receiving an injection for seven consecutive days. But I was not a civilian, I could not come out of the camp to get my injection every day. So, for the remaining six injections, I took them with me and a colleague actually in the camp administered one injection. He was the man who had never had anything to do with medicine or anything, but he was -- actually, I asked him and he agreed to give me these injections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, given that you later had to seek treatment, that these injections did not cure your tuberculosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, personally, I must say, I felt no effects. The pain remained the same and I was breathing very heavily and I do not think that the injections had any medical effects at all.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Judge Odio Benito, shall we break here? Good. We would like to ask Mr. Pasic to come back to the Tribunal at 2.30. The hearing is adjourned. (Luncheon adjournment) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, just 21 before the break you completed your testimony at least as far as answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. I will continue. Mr. Pasic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Before the break your testimony came to an end, at least as regards your answers. The Tribunal, I think, would like to take the opportunity of asking you some additional questions. Madam judge, do you have any questions you wish to put? JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Could you help me, please? Could you show this To the witnesses? (To the witness): Mr. Pasic, could you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us if you know why what the two large buildings were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first building held the prisoners and I was there too in the -- I never entered the other building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you went in that building. You saw more women than men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when that happened because I could not take a note of the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th of July in 1992 at 10 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that the women were mostly between the ages of 25 and 30; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most women who were there, between 20 and 25 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there children also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were children too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Small kids or young?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The children were mostly between three and seven years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there elderly people also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see many elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you saw any of the women getting beaten or the children, or the women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not beat the women. They only took them out. I do not know what they did once they took them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Nikolic himself took out three young women one night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same happened other nights or only one night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent only one night in the camp and that happened the night I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back for a moment to the school where you were first taken, you also said that they were mostly women and children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning they were mostly women and children and later a small number of men came there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any beatings of them of any kind, things against them, at that time in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did beat some of the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not beat the women. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Pasic about what he said concerning the cleansing of the town by a special unit under the chief, chief Vlado. If you remember, you said that he went and put house on fire and destroyed things and they came back very joyful. Now was this under Mr. Nikolic's supervision or was it completely independent from Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was independent of Mr. Nikolic, what happened in my town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was independent? Was it systematic? Were they doing things in an orderly way or was it just an act of violence with no purpose in itself? Did they have the purpose of, as they said, cleansing the town completely from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were acts of violence most likely planned beforehand, because they cleansed the town of everything Muslim, not only of the population, but also their houses, mosques, places of worship. They wanted to destroy everything that belonged to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were a police officer, you said you stopped a car which was full of JNA weapons, and then you had to let them pass by. Where do you think this car of JNA weapons came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car came from the Serbian part of the town and the weapons probably came from the JNA, because in that part of the town where the car came from, military trucks stopped very often, the JNA trucks stopped very often at that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these JNA trucks come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA trucks mostly came from the direction of Pale, north of my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Pale. Then you mentioned that at the camp in Batkovic there have been mass beatings by Serbian soldiers. Were they official soldiers, Serbian official soldiers, or citizens disguised as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilians disguised as soldiers who were tasked with guarding the camp. Anybody who was in a military uniform and stopped in the camp, stopped by, was allowed to go in and beat the prisoners and even kill them if he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were not under the orders of Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers in the Batkovic camp were not under the orders of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Pasic, before ending I would like to ask you some questions: First of all, could you perhaps recall more specifically Dragan Nikolic? What did he look like physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Dragan Nikolic was a middle aged man, about 30, 32 years of age. He was about 190 centimetres tall. He was not fat but he was well built and had a lot of muscles. He had dark brown hair. He did not wear a moustache or a beard and his eyes were bloodshot probably because of lack of sleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time when you were in Susica, do you remember the lighting at night? Was there a light on or was the hangar in complete blackness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent only one night in the Susica camp, not a month, not one month. The lighting ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are right, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the lighting within the hangar was very weak, very poor, but outside, especially around the wire that surrounded the hangar, the lighting was extremely good -- probably to prevent escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you wish to add anything to your testimony? Do you feel you have said everything you wanted to to this court and, if not, the Tribunal is fully prepared to hear anything you wish to add to your testimony in addition to what we have already heard from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have nothing else to say. What I have said is what I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to ask one question, maybe a clarification, from a prior question asked by your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Absolutely. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Pasic, when you were describing that you believed at least the soldiers who came into, I believe, Batkovic were civilians disguised as soldiers, could you explain exactly what you mean by that? For instance, did you mean that they never wore these uniforms other than to come into the camp, or do you mean they did not perform any military duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, during my time in Batkovic, all the civilian men between 18 and 65 years of age mostly wore military uniforms and weapons, military weapons, regardless of the time of the day or whatever their activity they were engaged in. All the male population was activated, was made ready, for fighting except that their tasks differed from one person to another. So they were not, in fact, civilians; they were soldiers who had fewer obligations than the soldiers on the front line and so they had more time to come to the camp and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Pasic, you have finished your testimony. The Tribunal thanks you once again for having come here and for your testimony which you have brought to us at the request of the Prosecution. Accompanied by the clerk, you can go back to the room that awaits you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the next witness I spoke with him just prior to the break and he has indicated that he wishes to testify publicly, other than his address not be given. So, as with the prior witnesses, I would ask that the protective order be lifted with respect to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Of course. We will take the same provisions as we have done for the previous witnesses, that is to say, we will know the identity and, please, then bring him into the room.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution call Hasim Ferhatovic. HASIM FERHATOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hasim Ferhatovic. Please remain standing for the moment so that you can read the oath which has been given to you in your mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth only the truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Ferhatovic, please be seated. Please do sit down. As I have told the previous witnesses, you are before the International Criminal Tribunal which is judging crimes against humanity committed in ex Yugoslavia, so you can express yourself and feel comfortable because you are within a legal centre. We fully understand the material and psychological difficulties linked to your testimony and, therefore, we will bear that in mind. If you have any difficulties at any moment during this hearing, please let us know. Madam counsel for the Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Hasim Ferhatovic. I was born in Vlasenica on 18th December. I lived there until the day when on 2nd June I was taken to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a nickname that you go by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Zoka" is my nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you gave your birth date, but does that mean that right now you are 46 years of age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the war what was your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed in the construction, Radnik Construction Company at Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was your full time job, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was full time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to working construction, before the war did you do any other kind of work on a regular basis, even if not on a full time basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I buried my neighbours in my free time. Sometimes I even had to ask for a day of to bury a friend, when a friend or a local resident died or when a neighbour of mine or a relative died, I would bury them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated you lived in Vlasenica your entire life up until you were arrested and brought to Susica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live with your wife and children in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived with my wife and my children and parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to your family, other than your wife and children, can you describe -- you have indicated you had parents -- did you also have brothers and sisters who lived in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica, there were five of us, five brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your family members help prior to the war when you would bury neighbours or friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my brother, Alija, and my father and I was there. Sometimes we needed a fourth man so Dzemal was also involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother Alija does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was called "Gico".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about when you were living in Vlasenica and were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home with my family, with my wife and daughter. My house was a little further away from my father's house, and when they came to pick us up a soldier, two actually, two soldiers arrived, Zoran Geguric, known as "Gegura" and Andjelko, "Kopitar", I know him by nickname only, but he used to be our postman and I would see him on a daily basis. So they told me, they said: "Who else is in the house?" I said, well, there was just myself, my wife and my daughters. Then they called me "Zoka", using my nickname. They said: "We must go to Luka, Luka, Susica. There is a meeting there", and I said: "Now, what will the women do if there is a meeting? Why would women go? Men should go alone". They said: "No, no, the women must come as well". So we went on. We marched in front of them. We came to a main street leading towards Susica, and when I saw that, the main street, I saw quite a number of people, large numbers of people, and behind our district, our part of the town, I saw lots of men having their hands behind their heads. And we were all walking towards Susica. When we came to Susica we were met by soldiers in different kinds of uniform, the uniforms of the former JNA, the uniforms of our police, the same kinds of uniforms that they had during the former Yugoslavia. Then women and children were immediately separated from us, and we men were searched, and they took from our pockets everything we had in the pockets. After that they threw us into the hangar. There I found my brothers, my daughters-in-law, my sisters-in-law, rather, children, my brothers' children. So we were locked there, and as we were entering the hangar we found people, women, and men in the hangar. I do not know exactly how many. I cannot give you the precise figure, but there were quite a number of people. We were not the first people to be brought there. That was the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the people there, of the people you recognised, did you know their religion or ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims, nobody but Muslims, and those that I met in already in the hangar, and I knew them, many of them. I saw them there as I entered the hangar. I recognised some people, and so we all of us felt very unhappy. We did not know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you met your brothers at the camp, how many of your brothers were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me and three -- and my three brothers. The only brother that was missing was my youngest brother who actually never left Vlasenica, but it was myself and my three brothers, Hajrudin, Dzemal and Alija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of your immediate family, meaning your wife and children, who was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was my father, my mother and my two sisters-in-law, and their children, the children of my sisters-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your wife and children also at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and one daughter, while my son had escaped towards Tuzla before that whole business started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe physically what Susica was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was a hangar belonging to the former JNA. It was used as a warehouse or an army depot usually for the weapons of territorial defence units. In fact, the hangar had been built by my company and I, in fact, as a worker, as a builder, was involved in the building of that hangar. This was simply a warehouse. There were two large doors of about four metres wide. There was a ramp, a loading ramp, when the trucks brought material or weapons, so they could approach that ramp and then unload. The building was about 40 metres long and about 20 metres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was commander of Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the Susica camp was Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known Dragan Nikolic before you got to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Dragan from his childhood, from his birth. I knew him. I knew his whole family. He worked in the Alpro factory at Vlasenica, he was a foreman, and we often were in touch. We would meet in the cafe in town. We were playing cards or billiards. He liked company and he liked the Muslim company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Nikolic while you were at the camp ever make any reference to your prior relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, never. He pretended he had never seen me before. Actually, on one occasion when we were there at Susica in the camp I used an opportunity or, rather, before, before coming to Susica, I actually buried his father when his father had died. His father was the slaughterhouse manager and I used to work there part-time, so we knew him and then I actually buried his father. And then he called me "Zoka", and he said: "Do not think that because you buried my father that you will have special privileges for that reason".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is something he said to you while you were at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your wife and children remain at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After four or five days the women, a certain number of women, they brought a book, somebody brought a book, and they asked the women to sign that they are leaving Vlasenica of their free will. Some of the women rebelled or refused, but then they threatened them with beating or killing unless they did that. So that they actually had to sign -- each woman had to sign that book. This was brought in by a Serbian clerk. I did not know him. There was a table at the exit from the camp. The book was there on that table, and there was a name of every woman, and she had to sign stating that he was leaving Vlasenica of her own free will. Then they were boarded on buses and trucks and lorries, and we heard that they were taken towards Kladanj, to the point, to the checkpoint of Luka. There they were left -- there they left the buses and they had to walk towards Kladanj on foot. Some people, like my father and other elderly people over the age of 60, these people were placed on trucks, also allegedly to be taken to Luka and to be sent to Kladanj but, unfortunately, they were not sent to Kladanj, rather, they were brought to the Srpske hamlet near Vlasenica, and that was controlled and surrounded by the Serbs, and these elderly people were sort of left there to die because there was no food there and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not before she left, your wife had to give up any property at the camp, any valuable property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I only learned that when I was exchanged. I knew that she had to give her earrings, she had to take them from her ear lobes -- my daughter as well -- but I did not see when this was happening. I only learned that from them, from my wife and daughter, when I was released, when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that you did not have any valuable property while you were at Susica, so you did not give up any valuable property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had something, I had my wedding ring, I had my wedding ring, and it was taken. It was taken from me when I was being transported to Batkovic. Then the ring was taken from my finger and money, I had some money, and this was taken away by a Seholje patrol which was escorting us to Batkovic. This was after leaving Susica towards Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your wife and children and some of the women left, were you and your three brothers still left at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remained in the camp and my three brothers. But the fifth brother, the last brother, was in the Vlasenica SUP prison, Vlasenica Interior Department prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time at Susica camp where you witnessed an event involved Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 21st June, sometime about 11.30 in the evening, during the night, then Dragan Nikolic and Goran Tesic, called "Goce", they actually walked into the hangar and brought out and took out Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. We had no reason why they were taken out. We only heard later because I was not far from the door of the hangar, the door was ajar, and they took them into -- towards the electricity pole. This was floodlit. First, they asked them questions and then they started beating them. As far as I could understand and hear, they asked Durmo: "Where is your son?" He said that his son had long lived in Ljublijana in Slovenia, and they asked him: "Where is your Kalashnikov rifle?" When I heard that, then after these words, suddenly there was thumping and beating. Dragan had a truncheon hanging from his belt which he used to beat people on frequent occasions. So, on that electricity pole there was a table plaque, there was a plaque, and there was a cup, there was a bucket and there was a spade, and so this was hanging from there. And then he was left, he broke the handle of the spade and with that handle, of the broken handle, of the spade, he would beat people on the back, on the head, until they fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "he" are you referring to Dragan Nikolic or Goran Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both. Both, in fact, both of them were beating them. You see, Goran took the spade and the other one used the pipe. He had a semi-automatic rifle which he left on the side, so he took the spade and he hit Durmo with the spade until the spade broke, so to speak. So the lower part fell off. Then later he took the -- Jenki Dragan took the pike and took the handle of the pike and then beat him, and then when he was finished he just threw the handle away, and then he went to sit at a table because there was a table there with chairs. Then they beat them also, kicked them also while they were lying on the ground. Then Dragan Nikolic called my brother, Alija. They asked him to pour a bucket of water over the two people to bring them back to consciousness. So he said to my brother, Alija: "Call somebody else from the hangar and carry them into the hangar" because they could not walk. Since I was close to the door, my brother actually called me and there was Ekrem Pasic and one more person whose name -- oh, yes, Smajlovic, Mirsad Smajlovic. So, the four of us, we took them by the arms and the legs and we brought them into the hangar. They had spent some half hour outside the hangar, but when we brought them back, I saw that Asim's head was all beaten. His eye was -- came out of his socket, so to speak. Blood, he was spitting blood and he was gurgling. He was suffocating. He lived for some 40 minutes after that and then died. While some 20 metres away from me other people were taking care of Durmo. They were wiping blood stains. They had some pieces of cloth to wipe him, and they put some compresses on him, cold compresses, but he was moaning and sobbing, so we had to tell Dragan that Asim had died. Then he said: "Well, you see, now, now you bury him according to your custom, you know how to do this". So we said: "We cannot do anything now; it was one hour after midnight. We will wait until morning". So we sat round him, around Asim, all night until the following morning. In the morning the door opened and Dragan Nikolic appeared in the door, and then he ordered me and my brother, Alija, to take the stretcher, the army stretcher, to take Asim out, carry Asim out of the hangar. So we took him out. We brought him to a warehouse, a nearby warehouse, where the packaging materials were loaded, and we wanted to bury him. Then I heard, while we were doing, he said to Mico Gojgolovic: "Go to the hangar and find a neighbour, Asim's neighbour, so that he would be sent to notify Asim's wife that Asim had died". So they found the first neighbour, the next door neighbour, of Asim, Meho Durmic, and together with Mico Gojgolovic, in his car, they sat in his car, and drove towards Asim's house to notify his wife of his death. They told the wife and she was told that that was a heart attack, and that he would be buried. So they came back. In the meantime, before they returned, we were waiting for the funeral car because they ordered -- they ordered the normal funeral car so that people would not feel what was happening, and Meho was not allowed to tell anybody that Asim had been beaten and that he had been actually killed because Mico Gojgolovic was with him, the Serb. So the wife came and stealthily, I was standing next to Asim, Dragan Nikolic was next to me, and when we saw, I said: "Let's see" -- this is Asim's wife -- she could not go into the camp, she was some 10 metres away from us, she was stopped. He would not allow her to come any further. She called my name, and said: "Hasim, has he suffered a great deal?" According to Dragan's orders, because he realised now, he said: "Tell her that he had not suffered at all, that it was a heart attack". So I said what he told me. I could not lie but I had to lie because I was forced for my own safety. So the woman left. She asked me to bury him in the Muslim cemetery not far from their house. I did that and when the funeral car came, the undertaker's car came, myself, my brother Alija, Mirsad Smajlovic and Ekrem Pasic, I think, but I am not sure, we went with that undertaker car. Four policemen followed us in the next car, and these four policemen, of these four policemen I only knew one which was Perica because he had his own private retail store in Vlasenica, so I knew him but I had not seen him here in the camp before. So they took us to the cemetery, the Muslim cemetery, in Vlasenica and they told me: "Now you do it according to your custom". So we buried the grave -- we dug the grave and, in the meantime, when we took Asim out, they say: "Just try to find a coffin or some kind of crate in the mosque". We could not find anything but we found a crate, an old box, wooden box. So we put Asim in there complete with his clothes, fully clothed. We buried him. We did not mark the grave at all. We simply covered the grave. They put us into the car again and returned us to the camp. While we were returning Perica stopped by at his retail store. He took about half a loaf of bread and some salami and gave us to eat. He said: "Do not eat here. You can eat when you come to the camp. There you can eat." While we were sitting outside, we just started eating the bread that we were given. We heard noise in the hangar. At that moment Durmo stripped to the waist, swollen all over his face, bare footed, no shoes on his feet, he was about to go to the entrance, to the way out of the hangar. The other people tried to stop him, not to get out, because Dragan was sitting outside, because he would otherwise beat him. At that moment Durmo fell down, collapsed on the floor. I came back to near the ammunition, the chest with ammunition, and I heard noise, they said: "He died". They immediately informed Dragan. Dragan was sitting in the shade near the guard house. He telephoned, Dragan telephoned the undertaker's vehicle and told us that we should go back and bury Durmo as well. We had no coffin. We just wrapped him in a blanket, a JNA blanket, and put a folium, olive coloured, and wrapped him and brought him to the cemetery and buried him, came back and that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to a Serb who was there part of the time, at least, I believe when you were waiting -- or who was involved in going to tell Asim Zildzic's wife, Mico Gojgolovic, was he a guard at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mico Gojgolovic was a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there was a Dzevad Saric at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, if anything, you saw happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was during the night, between the 23rd and the 24th June. Also, again Dragan Nikolic and Tesic Goran Goce, "Koke", they also called out Dzevad Saric and Muharem Kolarevic, also at the A post. I did not quite know why they had taken them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear anything after they were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite remember. I know they were taken out. Why they were taken out, I cannot remember at this point. My memory is failing me at the moment. They were taken out and they were beaten, beaten, beaten until almost they were made unconscious, and I saw that with my own eyes because the door was ajar, and I peeped through and I saw them shoot them dead with a machine gun, with a submachine gun. After they had killed them, then, as ordered by Dragan Nikolic, Koke came in to call me and my brother, Alija. We went out. I saw the men lying down. He also ordered us to take the stretcher and take them behind the hangar to remove them from there. We did so. First, we carried Dzevad Saric and then we came back and then Muharem Kolarevic too. Because the place where they were beaten was bloody, was covered with blood, he ordered us to take bucket fulls of water and wash away the blood. Because we could not wash away the blood because there was plenty of blood around, he ordered us to take sand, some sand, used for masonry work to cover it, and we covered everything, wherever there was traces of blood. We kept Dzevard on the stretcher. When we had finished all that, we asked them to go to the tap and wash our hands. Dragan was in the guard house. He had a military bed made of metal. His feet were on the bed. He was lying on the bed. Koke allowed us to wash our hands but he said: "Wait a little; there will be some more work for you." We had to stand by that guard house. He ordered my brother to go to the hangar and call out Zekic Ibro, nicknamed "Musa". I remember him clearly. He was also from the suburbs of Vlasenica. I knew him quite well. He was brought there. He came. He offered him a chair to sit on. He sat down, and he said: "Now tell us how you cut Milonja's throat". He starting swearing, by everything that he knew nothing about that, that he was drunk, that he was caught, that he is innocent, he knew nothing about it. "Now you will know whose throat you cut." There was a guard sitting next to him, an older man, about my age -- a little bit older than I am -- he had in his lap old German machine gun. He took that German machine gun and just emptied the barrel, the cartridge completely and riddled him with bullets and he just fell down from the chair. He said: "Go and get the stretcher".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he did this", do you mean Goran Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Goran Tesic ordered us to bring the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Goran Tesic the one who fired the shots shoots into Zekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Goran Tesic was the one who shot the bullets into Zekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Dragan Nikolic at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was inside, he was lying on the bed. It was a low window. There was a parapet of about 50 centimetres from the ground. That is where the guards lived, the guards who watched the prisoners. As we were on our way towards that place where he had -- we had left Dzevad Saric and Muharem Kolarevic, when we came there, we were stupified, we were shocked. Muharem Kolarevic was not the stretcher bearer, and we knew that we had left him there. I know that he was bloody, he was beaten up, badly beaten. I had seen that all with my own eyes, but he was not there. We came back, all in panic, and said we had not seen Kolarevic. They jumped up like wild wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they jumped up", who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan, Koke and all the other soldiers who were there. Dragan even jumped out of the window and, because they were panicked. Then they used flood lights to search for him and one of the Serbs then said: "You have hidden him." The other one said: "Where would they hide him? They cannot hide him in their pocket. They were there all the time". "It does not matter", he said. So we came back with the stretcher and picked up, lifted Zekic's body and took him next to Dzevard Saric's body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for one minute? How far away was the spot from where Musa Zekic was killed and then fell down from the guard house, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was sitting in the chair in front of Golan Tesic two metres from him, two metres from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away was the guard house where Dragan Nikolic was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The table was right next to the guard house. He was leaning with his back against the guard house and there was a chair in front and the other -- if you sat there, your back was against the wall of the guard house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Please go on. What happened after you put the body of Musa Zekic on the stretcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came back, we came back from that place. "Can we go back to the hangar?" we asked. They said: "Yes". He offered us some brandy. We could not, we were not -- we were afraid to say no, so we washed our hands. We had some brandy, washed our hands. As we were washing hands, we heard them saying: "We should call the police". Allegedly Dzevad and the other guy were supposed to be running away. He told us to go into the hangar and cover ourselves and, because the police were coming. Just as we entered the hangar I told everybody in hangar to lie down, not to sit down, the police were coming. We heard the noise of a car engine. The police were there. First there was silence and then the door was opened with a great noise. One of the policemen -- Dragan Nikolic came in, Koke and one of the policemen, whose names I do not know, who had come, who had -- whom Dragan and Koke had called. They said: "Which of you have tried to escape?" Nobody raised their heads. At the last moment an older man said: "Rasid Ferhatbegovic from Papraca". He could have been about 60 years of age. At that moment he was dozing off. He was scared and lifted his head. The policeman said at that moment: "Is that the one?" and Koke immediately responded: "Yes, he is the one". "Bring him over here". They took him out and we heard the sound of a gun shot. The door was closed. We could not see who did the killing. The door was closed again. There was silence until 5 o'clock in the morning. When dawn came at 5 o'clock in the morning, Dragan and Koke came to the door and said that I and my brother Alija should go out. We went out. "You know where the tools are for digging". We got the tools ready. They offered us a cigarette. We smoked a cigarette while waiting for a car which was supposed to come there. We thought we would drive them to the same place where we had driven Asim and Durmo to our cemetery. While we were smoking a small lorry came. It was driven by a manic named "Cadjo", which really means chimney sweep. He brought the car. In the meantime, I forgot to say, when we got up that morning, Tesic Goran told us: "Take the stretcher so you can see where that body is, the missing body is". We took the stretcher as we were going along the road where he was, we saw the blood and we saw wire, and then there was an outhouse. Muharem managed to where we had put him down and walk to the toilet to the outhouse, and the wire was mounted on concrete pillars, and beyond the wire there was forest and hill. He tried to go under that wire and walk out into the forest, at least that is my reconstruction. Then he bled. He must have got entangled in the wire and was hanging from that wire when we came there. I think he was dead already. Tesic, using the submachine gun with 36 bullets, round one way, one round the other way while he was dead. "Now", he said, "you can take him off; he will not run away any place". We barely managed to disentangle him. We tore some of his clothes in doing so and brought him to near where Dzevad Saric's body was and Musa Zekic's. Rasid Ferhatbegovic was also lying there. I just saw a hole, a small hole, in the forehead and it was black around that hole, and the part behind the forehead was not there at all. It was gone, disappeared. "Can we load him?" we asked, and they said: "Yes". A piece of the skull was there. He said: "Pick it up". He had a Russian beret on his head. I had to put everything in his hat. Everything, all pieces of his skull. When we loaded him, we asked him to go to the tap to wash our hands because our hands were bloody. They let us to do that. We got in the van, on the lorry, on the small lorry, and I thought we were headed towards the same place where we had buried Asim and Durmo, but the lorry turned into another direction. We kept driving. I know where it is. The place is called Mracni Do towards a village called Salokavja. I know, I know that area because I had walked around that area once. When they came to the curve at Mracni Do, "Now find a good place. You do not have to dig separate holes. You can put them all in one pit". It is woods, it is hard to find an area because there are a lot of roots. It is hard to find a place where you can put four bodies one next to another, because there is rock, there are roots, and we do not have the proper tools to do that. But they kept insisting and pushing us on and saying: "Hurry, hurry, hurry up". Wherever we started digging it was too hard to dig. Then I remembered at that place, at that area, they used to have quarries for limestone because they made limestone the traditional way from stone, and I knew that there was to be a cauldron there. Wherever there was metal there must have been a cauldron there. I found the cauldron. We cleaned it, maybe it was about 80 centimetres deep and one and a half metres and two metres in the sides. We asked if we can put him there. They said: "Yes". First, we put Dzevard's body and then Kolarevic's body and then later Zekic's body and Ferhatbegovic's. We put the earth on top of them, the ground. We found a tent of the olive green colour. We covered them with this tent -- the canvas, and then put the ground, and there was a little mound. We made a little mound. There were some trees around. I also put the trees on top of the mound. It was raining, it was driving rain. It was pouring. They told us to go back to the car. When we came to the Susica camp again, they gave us a hose to clean the blood on the lorry. When we finished washing, they gave us some of their own breakfast. I could not eat after what I had experienced. I just could not eat. I took what they gave me and gave it to somebody else. That roughly will be everything concerning this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Pasic a guard at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was, I might say, the right arm of Dragan Nikolic. They would never be separated. They never actually left the camp. It was only occasionally that they would leave during the day, but one of them was always left behind and the other would return very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Susica, in addition to the events that you have already told us about, did you witness any other acts of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Susica, I saw a bus, a blue bus. Birac was the forestry company and they had a bus for their workers, so I knew their blue bus, so that was the Birac forestry bus. The bus came once, stopped at the entrance to the camp. There is a little bridge there because the River Susica flows under that bridge. The bus stopped at the bridge and the bus was full of people. And Nezir Boric, Mevludin Hatunic, Hadzan, whose name I know only, I do not know his second name, he was the bus driver at the Bauxite Company, and Avdo who was the waiter at the bus station restaurant. So, these four or five people came and out. When they entered -- and the bus continued towards the place where I had buried Dzevard and Murahem. After some 10 to 20 minutes the bus came back empty. Later, an excavator, the yellow tractor excavator, also drove in that same direction towards that place, and when we asked Aldov and other people: "Who are these people?" Then they started telling us, they said: "They were the people who were in prison in the SUP Vlasenica", the police station of Vlasenica, "and we do not know what happened to them". I remember some of the names mentioned; Muharem Telalovic and his two sons, (indecipherable). Now, these were the names that we heard from these. Then there was a man, an Albanian man, who was a forester in our town. Some 35 people were actually in that bus. We heard later that they were killed, shot, and buried up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to inside Susica camp, did you ever see besides the incident you have already told us about, did you ever see Dragan Nikolic mistreat people in addition to the events you have already testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are witnesses, I think, the brothers Misad and Nurija. There were three brothers, the brothers Amir and Jakoop, Osmo and Bec, and he accused them of being the members of the SDA, the independent Muslim party, and he accused them of having weapons and said: "Where are the weapons? I will kill you if you do not tell me." So they were beaten every day, two to three times, on two or three occasions, and this was done by Dragan in person. He would use a truncheon. He had heavy boots, army boots. He would hit them and kick them and broke their ribs. Also, I saw him taking a knife, a bayonet, of an M45 rifle, and he would push that towards their throat to frighten them, and said: "Speak out, say where are the weapons?" or "Where is your brother?" In general, he always found some kind of reason to actually beat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people sometimes tied up outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the kind of punishment he would give. He would tie your two thumbs and you had to have your hands outside in the sun, and he would tie their hands by the drain, and the drain was higher up and the person would stand like this until he fainted. And then there were sharp stones on the ground and they had to kneel with bare knees. Then they would kneel, having their hand behind their heads until Dragan said that was enough. Dragan would just be sitting at his desk beating the time, so to speak, and waiting for the time to pass, whatever his pleasure was, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Susica camp, besides sometimes acting as grave digger, did you have to do any other sort of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We would leave around 7 o'clock in the morning. Goran would come, Goran Viskovic known as "Vjetar", nicknamed "Vjetar". He would come with the refrigerator, refrigerator lorry that had been used in peaceful times to transport meat in Vlasenica, and he said: "We need 20 people today. They have to do some work". So he would come into the hangar, Dragan followed and he just pointed the finger and said: "You, you, you and you" because he knew people from Vlasenica. So he would collect 22 people, he took 22 of us, and put us into the refrigerator, lorry but the lorry was not refrigerating. It was simply suffocating but not cold. He would take us to a farm near Vlasenica where we gathered livestock, built fences for livestock so that livestock would not escape. Then we also have to work in our gardens. We had to dig, to work in the gardens so they could collect and harvest the produce. All kinds of things we did. Some people worked. There is a place call Lage where they were building a new barracks. That was done by a group of people. It was always like this. We started around 7.00 in the morning and were brought back about 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. So they would come again at 7.00 the following morning, took us to work. We were given a slice of bread, and only if the guards were more merciful they would give us some of their food, but otherwise we just got a slice of bread for 24 hours -- today at 10 o'clock in the morning and then again tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe while you were at Susica how you reacted to this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
