utterances.text: How do you react when you see it all happening; people being brought in, reading your names from lists, some people, and then everything has to go to Dragan and then it is said: "Now these people are called for interrogation", but these people would be taken away and never brought back. Where they ended, we just did not know but they never came back. Whoever was taken away, anybody that was taken away, had to be approved by Dragan Nikolic. So for anything that happened, any kind of, anybody being taken away, he had to give his approval. I watched on a number of occasions people being taken away and never brought back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself frightened while you were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you see what is happening then you simply wait when your turn will come. Will your turn come? You think all kinds of thought. What I have done in my life? Have I have ever done anything? Will somebody come who remembers a long kind of history to torture you? But, thank God, nothing happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when some prisoners were sent from Susica to Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the first group left on the 27th June. That was the first group for Batkovic. There were people from Kalesije and Papraca, also some people from Vlasenica. They simply wanted to fill one bus load. The second group left on 28th June again for Batkovic. They were all people from Vlasenica. I was in the third group on 30th June but I was not in the hangar. That morning, on 30th June, Goran Viskovic came and took us to work in a field, in a corn field, and there were 22 of us, including my two brothers, Alija -- sorry, not Alija, Dzemel and Hajrudin. So we waited for this piece of bread for our lunch, but instead of this a policeman came with short sleeved shirt, said: "Leave your tools there and go into the refrigerator truck" in which we were transported. So we wondered what was happening now. We knew there was another group to be sent to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that the groups of people leaving were being sent to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew it from Mico Gojgolovic. He told me personally. He said: "This is your only salvation. If you can be sent to Bijeljina, because if you remain in Susica", he said, "you will all get killed", and fronts opened, fighting began. Their people were also killed in the war, and they would come as wild dogs into the Susica camp and then took people away, they maltreated them, they beat them, some people were killed, of course, and so they were simply taking revenge upon us for their losses on the battle, in the battle field. So he told us: "The best thing that can happen to you is to be sent to Batkovic". That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a guard at the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a guard, yes. He, in fact, was the only one that you could approach and speak to him. I must say, even to this High Court, he never beat anybody, he never did anything to anybody. I cannot say but what is right. He may be rich but that is another problem. He would go with his own car and would bring cigarettes to us, but he was despised by his other friends but he was not afraid. He always quarrelled with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the two brothers went with you when you were brought to Batkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My two brothers Hajrudin and Dzemel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides you and your two brothers who was left at Susica at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Susica, Alija and Maludin were left; Alija Gico and Maludin, nicknamed "Mijka". They remained at Susica. My sister, Alija, and my brother-in-law, Ibro, and I must say until the present day we know nothing about them. We do not know whether they are still alive or not -- nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about why any of them were not sent to Batkovic with the other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see your brother, Gico, scheduled to go to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was supposed to leave in the first group on 27th, he was scheduled to go. He actually was in the bus already, but there was somebody reading from a list of names and Dragan Nikolic was there and, in fact, he read my brother's name, and so as we entered the camp they had the list of our names and it is from this list that they decide who will go to Batkovic. So, my brother was supposed to leave on 27th in the first group, so his name was called and he sat in the bus. Then people said: "Oh, Gico is leaving". At that moment, Dragan Nikolic heard this, heard this "Gico is gone". And then he did not know my brother, he knew my brother not as "Alija" but as "Gico". So at that point he went into the bus again and took my brother out of the bus and said: "You are going to stay here", and so he did stay -- until today perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Batkovic for 13 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the conditions at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Horrible, horrible conditions, especially for the first two months. Our arrival, when we came there, they were beating us, they mistreated us. They cut our hair, their shaved our heads, in fact. They kept us in the sunshine, in a closed, in a camp with barbed wired, some five or six rows of barbed wired, with sentry boxes and observation points with machine guns, with search lights, and all of this was pointed towards the camp where we were gathered like ants. So we were beaten, maltreated until the point when the International Red Cross arrived. When the International Red Cross arrived, then it was a bit easier, I must say. The International Red Cross intervened. Then they allowed us to come out accompanied. We went to harvest their grains, and this was done for Serb peasant. Anybody who had anybody in the Yugoslav army was entitled to take requisition prisoners who would then be collecting, harvesting maize, potatoes, hay, cutting hay, drying hay. When we came to a farmer, we were given food as we worked, and that was life until the 21st of July 1993 when I was exchanged and freed together with my brothers and my father, because my father also came to Batkovic later from Srpska. I did not say before. My relatives, my mother and wife and children, thought that my father was at Tuzla and they told us so. But my father was not in Tuzla, but they were not allowed to write the truth. We thought now my father was in Tuzla, suddenly you see him in prison, a man aged 70, and then this was really shocking and horrifying. When they left Srpske, he was captured there at Batkovic. Then he was taken to Zvornik where he spent six months. When he was supposed to be exchanged, then he was brought to Batkovic instead. He stayed there between 8th February 1993 to 21st July 1993 when he was exchanged together with me, the man of 70 years with heart attack, partially paralysed. I had to take care of him.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have any additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] It is now 4 o'clock. I suggest that we adjourn for 30 minutes this time. So we will continue with the witness at 4.30. (Short Adjournment). 4.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We can resume the hearing. Judge, would you like to raise some questions of the witness? JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Ferhatovoic, if you do not mind I would like to know how is your family right now? How is your mother, your wife, your sisters-in-law, how are they all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother died. I did not find her alive when I came back from the camp. My wife and my children are OK. They are living with me. I visit also my two sisters-in-law, the wives of my brothers whom I have lost. I also visit the son of my sister who has also gone. They are of course sad. My brother who was killed who is missing, the son keeps asking me: "When will my father come?" and I said: "He will come back. Probably he will be exchanged as I was exchanged." We live on in Tuzla. We help each other as much as we can. If I have anything extra I give it to them and they give to me if they have anything they can spare. We just co-operate very well, help each other. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Ferhatovoic, you mentioned that Nikolic used to invent a pretext to torture people and to enjoy watching the torture, but some torture was done by others of course. Was it all the torture and the killing under his command or do you think things were done sometimes without his being involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I could see everything that happened in the camp, in the Susica camp, everything derived from him. Whoever started doing something he would be there to continue the beating, and I think everything originated from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question, you said that you went to work to build fences and barracks. Were these barracks related to the war activities and were you engaged to work in the field of the battle or was it work independent from the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the work related to the frontline was done while I was in the Batkovic camp. I went to Miovica mountain and chopped wood for the Serbian soldiers. While I was in Vlasenica, when I worked there, when I did those fences for the cattle, they gathered cattle, livestock, because livestock was simply left to their own resources and they would just close in all the livestock. But the force labour in Batkovic was related to the military. I dug trenches, loaded ammunition. I did all sorts of things. I also worked on the transmission lines, everything. Even we chopped wood for their families in their houses. They did not want to chop their own wood. We had to chop wood for them, firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you exposed to danger in this work, danger coming from the battles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There were cases of people who got killed, who were killed because he was hit by a sniper on the other side, because he does not know who I am; he just looks for somebody to kill and he does not know whom he kills because a grenade does not chose where Serbs are. It just hits a place and whoever happens to be there gets killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact you were on the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also you mentioned that anybody who had someone in the Yugoslav army could take prisoners from your camp to use whatever, to use them in whatever they wanted. When you say "anybody who had someone in the Yugoslav army", which Yugoslav army are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav army, whoever had anyone in the battlefield, old men and weak people remained behind, the Serbian people, they went to the command, to the Serbian command, and asked for permits for people, for 10 or 20 men to be taken out so that these people from the Batkovic camp, that is us, we would help with the harvest, with the potato harvest, chop wood, because he was old and his son was on the frontline in the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the Serbian army, paramilitary army, controlled by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last, there was some statement you said that when they were transferring people you said they transferred old people and left them at an unknown place for them to die. Did I understand rightly that the old people were transferred and were left and nobody found them after that and they were left to die? I noted it down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they transferred people from the Susica camp, women, old people, 60, 65 years old and older, they took some of them, drove them towards Kladanj and others they took towards Cerska; it is a village called Cerska, which was surrounded by Serb forces, Serbian forces, and Muslims lived in Cerska itself in the village. There were people who died there because they had no medication, not enough food, they did not have a doctor around to protect them, protect their health. I know, according to my father who told me, who lived there in Cerska, he told me about, individually about people who died because they could not endure the conditions. Some of them lacked medicines and no food or medicine could come because the village was surrounded by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who sent them there -- was it Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Nikolic with his associates. There was a commission set up headed by Dragan and they decided who will go where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Ferhatovoic, was your sister at the camp at the same time as you? I believe that was the case. Here is the question. What happened to the women during the period when you were at the Susica camp? How many women were there? What did you observe happening to them? What was done to these women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was able to see two or three times while I was there during the one month I spent there, they took the women out, young women, I do not know their names. They took them out in the evening and brought them back in the morning. Where they took them, what they did, but judging by the way they appeared, because they came back full of tears, with their hair tousled and their clothes torn, what they did I could not tell exactly, but I did see them being taken about 8, 9 o'clock in the evening and bring them back before 7 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time whilst your sister was with you was it possible for you to communicate with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was life like in the village before the war? Was life peaceful or was it possible to note and feel the tensions between the different communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I want to say where this hatred came from for us. Although for years, as if we had hated each other for years, but there had been no quarrels, no fighting or even at various gatherings in dance halls there had never been any fights, all of a sudden out of the blue for no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was quite sudden? There was nothing which would indicate this would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was totally mysterious. Why? We kept asking "Why?" Because until previous day we used to visit each other, socialise, had drinks together, ate food together. If he bore a grudge against me I would have understood that, but there was nothing of the kind. For him to hate me so much that he can kill me, I just could not believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question. I would like to ask you now, given what you have seen and all that you have suffered, you have buried a lot of dead people, you have seen a lot of death witnessed, a lot of suffering, you are now giving a public testimony. What are your feelings here and now today? What are your emotions and feelings at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment I came here to tell the truth and it is a painful truth because of my two brothers and my sister mostly, and because of my entire nation which suffered, which went through an ordeal to tell the real genuine truth what these criminals did to us. I would not have the courage to conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Ferhatovoic, the Tribunal thanks you very much indeed for your appearance here in The Hague before the International Tribunal. At this point your testimony is complete, and the Clerk will show you out to the room which is waiting for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We have spoken to the 17 next witness we propose to call. This witness has indicated that he does not wish to have any orders made in respect of concealing his identity or evidence. I would ask that the order for non-disclosure in respect of this witness be lifted, except in so far as it might apply to his address being disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes. Mr. Registrar, please note the request and also the answer which is along the lines, the same answer to the request made previously by the Prosecutor for the previous witnesses. So please introduce the next witness. Please tell us his name, his family name and first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Suad Mahmutovic. SUAD MAHMUTOVIC, Called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Can you hear me? Mr. Mahmutovic, can you hear the interpretation? If so please remain standing and read out the solemn declaration which has been given to you. Please read it out to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare I will speak the truth and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your full name is Suad Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, if I could speak directly To the witness. Mr. Mahmutovic, you have appeared before the International Criminal Tribunal. We would like to invite you to speak calmly in your testimony and we would like to assure you that we can guarantee your protection in this institution. If you have any difficulties whatsoever please communicate these to the Tribunal. We are very aware of the courage that you have shown in agreeing to be a witness and coming to this Tribunal to tell us about your experience during previous months and years. Counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your full name is Suad Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on 29th August 1955?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Zvornik but I lived in Vlasenica all my life. All my live I lived in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation in Vlasenica before 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the aggression on Bosnia, I worked as a lorry driver and also a shop owner. I owned a shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, I would ask you if you would to cast your mind back to 4th May 1992 when you were at your residence, and could you tell me the events that followed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 4th May 1992 I was at my home. Goran Viskovic, Viskovic nicknamed Vjetar, took me to the police station. When he brought me to the station he asked me how I had armed Muslims in Muslim villages and gave me a piece of paper to write on it. I said I did not do anything of the kind. I can only confirm that I bought wood from Serbs in a village called Zalicovic where I can say, I can confirm that the only truth is that I bought wood from them when he told me to take a piece of paper and write. I took the piece of paper and wrote. When I wrote what I had in mind, what I thought was true ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you write on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote that I had been buying wood from Serbs, that I had not engaged in any armament or nor did I sell any weapons, because he said if I did not write the way it was I would be killed. When I wrote that he took my statement, Goran Viskovic nicknamed Vjetar, and left it there. They let me go home, which I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where was the police station that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the centre of the city; in the centre of the town near the bus station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the centre of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went home. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day in the evening, about 11 o'clock in the evening, it could have been about 11 o'clock, I saw a car that was parked outside my house. There were three Serbian soldiers. One of them got out and cocked his submachine gun. They were standing there and I was frightened. I do not know how long they stayed there; it could have been 15 or 20 minutes and then they left. The following morning I was ordered to report at the police station, which I did. When I came to the police station I had to report to Ljuban Stanisic. I found him he took me into his office. We sat at a table, at a desk. He took out, he pulled out a drawer and took my statement out of it. "Suad, since I know you well, we went to school together, I am going to tear up this statement because you said you had no weapons. I will let you go home and don't let anyone say anything against you." "You know me, Ljuban", I said to him, "I have never done anything wrong." I went home from there. I was of course panicked. I came home. I told my wife that I had to get a permit for us to leave the town. She said, "Go ahead." I went with my relative called Naser Zildzic. I was told to come there at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you told to go at 12 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the municipality building, to where those permits were issued, those passes. I cannot remember his name. I went home. I told my wife everything. I told her I was told to go there at 12 o'clock. I went to my sister's place with my cousin Naser to have coffee with her. We had coffee and then left to go home. At that moment a car came and there was a hoot, a horn of the car sounded, and there was a Dragan Bjelanovic in it. He motioned to us with his hand to come to him. We came up to him. He was wearing camouflage uniform. "Who is Zildzic Naser?" he asked, and "Mutacic Suad?" I said: "I don't know anything about Mutacic Suad." He said: "Get into the car and show him, point him out to me." "Can I see the paper?" He says: "It's not Mutacic. It's Mahmutovic Suad." "Well, then we are looking for you exactly. Get into the car." He started mistreating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we got into the car", who was "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was myself and Naser Zildzic, my cousin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man Rikanovic, what position was he? What was he, a soldier, policeman or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rikanovic was a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had a list of names, did he, in the car with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the names of two of us. He was actually looking for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took us in his car to the police station where I told him, "But why are you bringing me there? I have been to the police station?" He says: "Well, we must check something on you." So we started. When we came to the second floor he brought us to Ljuban. So he first called Naser Zildzic. I listened at the door. Ljuban Stanisic told him: "Now what kind of weapons are you trading?" Now Naser claimed that that was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for a moment, Ljuban Stanisic, what position was he in? What position was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes. I would say that he was the main one who was actually interviewing Muslims when they were brought. He decided who was to be arrested or imprisoned and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think he was? Did you think he was a policeman or a military person or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was an agent. It is difficult. I cannot tell you really, but he was very powerful because he could order people to be brought to the police station to be detained. That was done on his orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course he was a Serb and a great Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he first started interrogating your cousin Naser Zildzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is exactly the way it was. Naser, when he finished interrogating Naser he called me in. He said: "Listen, I let you go and now you continue to trade in weapons." I said: "Ljuban, listen, I didn't sell anything. I went to the municipality for the permit. My child is sick. I want to leave the town. Look at me." He said nothing. "I don't want to talk to you. I thought you were a man, but you are not." I told him: "Ljuban, come on, I didn't do anything at all and you know it." So he picked up the telephone and called a policeman and ordered him: "Take him". So the policeman took me to the corridor where they had a cell, this was in the police station. At that was the normal police station cell. They closed me there, they locked me up. The door was black iron door, and there was only full board iron door, and there was only a small hole through which I could look inside. This was a small room, some two and a half metres by two metres, and there were already 20 people there. Then there was a sort of impossible space for 20 or 22 people to live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ljuban Stanisic was a friend of yours before the war, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was my school mate. I went to school together with him, same class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It is difficult to say. An awful thing happened. The whole thing changed, people changed suddenly as if we had not known each other. We were looked down upon as the lower case. I do not know what they wanted to do to us, who we were, what kind of nation, with whom we had been living. We had lived together, we went to school together. We shared good and bad in our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the time you were put into that small cell of 2.5 metres by 2.5 metres, what happened after you were put into that very small cell with the 20 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they brought me to the cell I saw people there who were not able to sit because there was no room. They were standing. I knew some of these people. I did not know others. There were some three to four people from Bratunac who were taken off the bus heading for Tuzla. So I asked people, "What happened to you? When were you brought in?" I talked to people who I did not know but we became sort of acquainted with each other. We asked them: "What are you doing? What are they doing to you?" They say: "Oh, my brother, keep quiet. If you open your mouth you'll get killed." That is what they told me. We could not sleep. If you lie down, if you lay down then somebody had to lie on top of you or you on top of his feet or legs, and if somebody pressed the lock or the door knob we had to stand up immediately and lower our heads. Two cousins beat us every day. We had to urinate in that cell. If you asked to be taken out you would be met by three to four Serbian soldiers who would beat you. So it was better to simply urinate where we were, where are closed and locked. It was better that than being taken out. Maltreatment happened on a daily basis. Of course we could not even ask for cigarettes. We breathed in this room. This was a small opening, 15 by 20 centimetres. That was the only ventilation, and for 15 days some 20 people were breathing the air that came through that hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you just mentioned that during that time you were mistreated during those 15 days. You were beaten during that period, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, everybody and every day. I was beaten on a daily basis by Serbian soldiers. Whether he was an employee or a soldier, the door would open, they said: "Let us see now who was there." They would open the door and then without choosing young, older people, they did not choose the tools. They kicked us. They had so-called boxes, the iron grips which you put on your fingers and they would hit you. This was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "iron grips", can you give us a more detailed description of the iron grips they had on their fingers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the knuckles that you put on your fingers and there was a hole you put your fingers through the hole and the metal was there on top, and then they would hit you; they would hit you in the chest. Of course people would faint. They were screaming and we could hardly hear. We all shivered standing there and listening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from punching you with their fists with iron grips on their fingers, did they hit you with anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this cell this was mainly beaten by kicking, and they were the Serbian criminals. This was not a man like me who was frail. They had to be very strong people and very stout people so they could torture us as much as possible, injure us as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these guards were solders or whether they were police that were beating and the other people in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Garic, the two cousins Garic, were Serb policemen. They were called policemen or special policemen. They had colourful masks, camouflage uniforms. When the Muslims were brought for interview, not in the cell, but outside of the cell. They would then say, "Now you Serbs be careful the green berets are coming." At first I did not understand this. This was the first time I heard the term "green berets". Then they brought a man who was a civilian person, never a soldier, and we asked him, "What are you?" He said: "I am a Muslim and nothing else and who are the green berets?" Well, nothing, they just wanted to kill me because they called me a green berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever understand later what was meant by the term "green beret"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still do not quite know what they wanted to say. I had never seen the green berets before that. You might have had a green beret or blue beret or white beret, I do not know. I never realised whether they wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On one occasion were you beaten by, beaten with a baton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten because first of all I spent 15 days in SUP and then I was taken to prison which is across the street from the SUP, next door to the court house, 100 metres away from the police station. That is where I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that an occasion when you were beaten with a baton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was brought to the prison I remember very well there was a man called Amirkana, a person with whom I spent a lot of my time. He was also a car owner or lorry owner, and on one he asked the guard to open the door for him. He asked me for my name, by my nickname Gazija, and since we had spent a lot of time together I was hoping that he would help me, to bring me cigarettes, to see what he could do for me, but he actually put his hands behind his back, then he revealed his baton hanging from the belt, and he asked me to step out and I did that. Then: "Give the gun, give the rifle that you have." I said: "I have no rifle. I was at the police station. They know I have no rifle." He said: "Give the rifle and enter the toilet" and I had to do this. But before that I told him, I said: Bastah, listen, our friendship has been trampled on." He said "We have never been friends at all." So I entered the toilet. This was a bathroom you might say and this was a concrete trough, and he started hitting me with the baton until I fainted. I did not count, but people who were in the room, kept in the room opposite that, two metres away, they herd all the thumping, and a man told me later that I had been hit 85 times with the baton. I could hardly believe I could not faint before. Then they gave me cold compresses and so on because when we were beaten, myself or my neighbour or any other Muslim man, we helped each other when they returned. One had to watch through the hole in the door to see that the guards were not in the front of the door, but we were helping each other. We had water, cold water we put on the part of the body which was injured so that the swelling would be eased and would be less and so on. People were beaten on a daily basis. It was horrible. Unknown people came with masks or socks, stockings over their faces, 45 people from Bratunac had been taken away, and they were taken towards Nova Kasava. These people were all shot and killed. One survived and I hope that he can come to this court to testify about 45 people killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall one day when the ICRC came to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date, but a younger woman came and a man. We heard them saying to the Serb soldiers: "Can we visit these people, the detainees?" and the Serb officer said "Yes". When they entered they identified themselves and they asked the Serb guard to leave the room so they could talk to us in private. He left but when he closed the door he remained at the door and tried to listen to what was being said. We were asked why we were brought here, by whom. We told them this was an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Serbs. We were asked whether we were beaten, maltreated, whether we were receiving food. When they saw that we were sleeping on the concrete floor and so on, on naked floor, they said: "Listen, we will try to protect you. We protect human beings." So we told them: "Look at where we are living, how we are sleeping." Then Bjelanovic came, the former head of the local police, and he said: "What are you doing here?" he said turning to me. I said: "I have no idea. How do I know? Can you do something for me to get me out?" He said: "But I must see to it that you are released. Why you be imprisoned?" I said: "I have no idea. How do I know?" Kadija Subasic was also with me and he said: "Where do you come from?" He said: "I am from Zepa". "Where do you live? " There was the village called Yezora not far from Vlasenica, and he says: "What is Jusuf?" "Jusuf is my brother." "Ah," he says: "That is the one, the Croatian Ustasha defence forces slaughtering Serbs in Zepa." The brother said: "No, I don't know anything." So they started hitting him. When the International Red Cross had completed the interview and Bjelanovic left with them, they gave us a pack of Camel cigarettes, I remember the brand. When they left we had more problems. They said: "Now you are looking for help and assistance. You balija fucking mothers, nobody will ever help you." I then felt it might have been better if the Red Cross had never come because they asked us: "Now what did they ask you? What did you tell them? You don't like us Serbs. You inform against us." We said: "No, we just told them about our life and so on."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened you to after that? Were you beaten after the Red Cross had come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, it was worse. When the Red Cross had left the problems appeared, beatings, they beat me, and everybody else in the room because there were in fact three rooms in the prison. We told ourselves: Why did they come at all? Had they not come it would have been at least the way it was before and not so bad as it was now. That day when the Red Cross had left Kadija had new problems. In the evening around 10 o'clock we had no electricity in the prison. So then somebody knocked on the door. Kadija and I were alone. There were some shelves there and I tried to hide in the shelf, and Kadija was invited to come out. Apparently his wife was there. He said: Why the wife be coming to see him in at 10 o'clock in the evening? That is impossible. But they took Kadija and I heard the guard say, "We will cut his throat by Sekovici, the fucking bastard." So I remained there alone. I groped my way and I was simply listening for the door to open, but Kadija never came back. The following morning, I do not know what time it was, they brought him back half alive, half dead. They threw him into the room. He could not move his limbs and when they left, the Serb soldiers left or Chetniks, then we came to his help. We took his clothes and I asked him: "Kadija, who beat you?" He said: "Well, Garic. They beat me with the chains. They had trampled on my chest." He was so weak that we only made his lips wet and did not allow him to drink anything or swallow anything. This was quite horrible. When I saw Kadija I was deeply shocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the prison I think it was the 10th, 15th June, but it was June, until June, June 15th. Then we were transferred. I was transferred one day, it was in the month of June when they came. They read the names, read out the names, 20 of us, including my brother Nurija who had also been in prison with me, the same prison. They read the names out. They took us outside and we saw Czar with a flag. We were loaded on to the car and the canvas was tied up and the car went on, the truck, and we were brought to the SUP building. Then they put Zekic on the same truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken, we were driven, after they put Salih Zekic on, we were taken to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Susica camp, can you tell me what you recall about the day you arrived at that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the Susica camp, the car was parked within the perimeter of the camp. I saw my neighbours. I knew them all. I saw Dragan Nikolic. He had two hand grenades, a submachine gun and a bayonet. When we got off the truck we had to go in a single file to the place where we were to be registered. It was like a registry, just up from the hangar where they stayed. They had to write our names. I saw Velko Basic, a former Yugoslav policeman. He wrote our names and surnames. We go back to the hangar. There I saw my neighbours from Vlasenica and also people from Croatia. The hangar was full was crammed, about five or 600 people. It was horrible. One day came -- one day went by and nobody touched me. Well, then the next day came with many, many problems. Dragan Nikolic came into the hangar and looked for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position Dragan Nikolic had in the camp, what position he held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were about to tell us about something that happened to you when Dragan Nikolic came. Continue on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came into the hangar he called my name, and two brothers of mine, Mirsad and Nurija: "Get out of here, you Balijas mother fuckers" which we had to do. He took us outside the hangar where there was some pebble -- gravel, and we had to kneel down on that gravel, very sharp gravel, and put our hands behind our head .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, we have a little technical problem and we 16 have missed a little part of your evidence. I am sorry about this. Would you mind going back a little bit and start telling us from the time you had to have your hand behind your head? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The French interpretation was fine. But go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes, we had to put our hands behind our head. When he took us out in order of age, I was born in 1955 Nurija in 57, and Mirsad was born in 59, and they told us to stand according to our age, one next to another. They said: "Kneel down" which, of course, we had to do, "Keep your -- hold your hands behind your back" which we also did. Yes, he told us to spread our feet. It was very, very hard and rough on us because the gravel was very sharp. We moved a little bit. They said: "Do not move, I am going to slit your throats." He started beating me. The chessboard, which is the sign of the Croatian coat of arms, "Where is the chessboard?" I said I had no chessboard. I do not know what "Sahomnica" is. "Sahmonica" is the Croatian word for the chessboard. "We will bring the door from the trucks so you can see what a sahomnica is". If there is a Sahmonica on my door, I will kill myself".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying they were saying that on the door of your truck was the Croatian symbol, is that what you were saying? They were accusing you of having that on the door of your truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they accused me, which was not true, and I was very, very definite about it, that it was not true. I claimed with all responsibility it was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was accusing you of having the Croatian flag on your truck door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was accusing me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I interrupted you. Continue on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He started beating me. When he start beating my brother, Mirsad, I pleaded with him: "Please do not hit him. He has one kidney missing." Well, he enjoyed that almost. "Show me where is that missing kidney?" Then he hit him right there, and he immediately fainted. Then he continued to walk over us, all the three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parts of your body were you hit during this beating, what parts of the body did they hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, here, you can see this is from his foot, he broke seven of my ribs in this area. He pushed his -- the barrel of his handgun, 7.62, and just got my teeth out with the gun. Every day he beat me with his hands. He kicked me. The method was when we fainted there was a bucket full of water which they poured over you. If you made the slightest move with your head, they would say: "Oh, Balija is still alive". When they had enough, he ordered the guards to throw me back into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he put the pistol into your mouth, did he do anything with the pistol other than just put it into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he held the barrel of the gun in my mouth he kept pulling the trigger, and saying: "Tell me who has the weapons" and cursing me all the time, offending me nationally. I said: "I do not know. You can kill me but I do not know."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a detainee from Kula-Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do quite well. But I do not know his name. But I know he was from Kula-Grad near Zvornik. I remember the guard, Bece(?) and Krune and Cane, two brothers, Krune and Cane. I do not remember the date. They brought him. Dragan Nikolic ordered that he be hit which they had to do. They beat him. They kicked him with the -- they hit him with the rifle butts. He watched several minutes. At one moment he said: "What kind of Serbs are you, you can't even kill him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic. He uncocked the submachine gun and fired a round of fire. Of course, he killed him with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your uncle in the camp with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. My mother's brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim Zildzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident with your uncle and a man called Durmo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember quite well. I do not know the date, the exact date, but it was about 11 o'clock in the evening, 12.00 maybe, when they took them out. They took them outside. They beat them with handles, with axe handles. They moaned, they screamed, they yelled. I do not remember for how long it went on. They brought them and dumped them back into the hangar. When I saw that his eye had come out of his socket, Ferhatovoic Hasim and somebody else came up to him. They put him up against the wall because he could not walk, he could not stand on his feet. I also walked up to him and Hasim told me: "If they see you, they will take you out and will kill you" and I did so. I think about half an hour after that they say he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the person with the eye out of its socket, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother's brother, Zildzic Asim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the other person, Durmo, who was taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Durmo survived that night -- he died, I am sorry, he died in the afternoon about 2 p.m. the following day. He was buried by Hasim Ferhatovoic with his brother Alija, nicknamed "Gico".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Prosecutor counsel, it is as you wish, it is also up To the witness. I would like to explain this To the witness now. Normally speaking, we finish at 5.30. If you would prefer to carry on for a little while longer, that is fine, together with the Prosecuting counsel, until quarter to six, otherwise we can come back at 10 a.m. tomorrow morning, and in that way the witness could have a restful evening this evening. It is really up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness might indicate what his preference would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] It would be desirable for me to take a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Fine. Then we would like you to come back to see us tomorrow to continue your testimony, so I thank you very much, Mr. Mahmutovic, we will come back tomorrow for 10 a.m.. (The proceedings adjourned until the following day)
